STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER ON DELETION OF VOTE IN COURSE OF DIVISION, MAY 22
speechtext:
When the house divided yesterday on Mr. Cockeram's motion for production of certain papers, Mr. Bracken (Leader of the Opposition) rose from his seat and his name was called by the Clerk Assistant and recorded by the Clerk, who repeated Mr. Bracken's name. This repetition of a member's name is an announcement to the house that the member's vote has been recorded. The Clerk is sworn to record the res gestae on things done in the house. When another member's vote, namely Mr. McGregor's, had been recorded and duly announced, Mr. Bracken rose again and stated he had voted inadvertently as he had been paired with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) during the latter's absence in England. He suggested that his vote be deleted, and the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Usley), the leader of the house (Mr. Mackenzie), and several other members agreed that this should be done. No opposition being taken, the Clerk then rubbed off the mark he had made opposite Mr. Bracken's name, which was not included in the division list.
Privilege-Mr. White (Hastings)

The Clerk's action was not a new departure. Bourinot, 4th edition, page 382, says:
In the Canadian Commons the Clerk at the table has been on more than one occasion allowed to strike off the name of a member who is recorded and then admits having been" paired.
In 1926, when Mr. Bird voted though he had been paired, he announced his error after the result of the division had been given out and the Speaker had declared the motion carried. There was no possibility at that time of making any correction and the Speaker was right in refusing to allow that the vote be withdrawn. The Speaker then said:
The rule is that when a vote has been recorded, when the result has been proclaimed and when the motion has been declared carried or lost, that expresses the judgment of the house.
-and he refused to entertain Mr. Bird's request that the recorded vote be deleted. Had Mr. Bracken's request been made after the house's decision had been declared by the Speaker, it would certainly have been refused, but I see no objection in having his name struck out immediately after he had inadvertently voted.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Speaker, if I may say so, by consent of the whole house, I am sure that the conduct of the leader of the opposition was of the most honourable kind.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER ON DELETION OF VOTE IN COURSE OF DIVISION, MAY 22
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like to compliment you upon making a most intelligent ruling on the incident. If the time ever comes when the rules of this house preclude the withdrawal of an inadvertent vote when the obvious intention was clear, it is time that the rules were altered. I compliment Your Honour upon your decision.
Mr. M. J. COLBVvELL (Rosetown-Biggar): Mr. Speaker, as the member who raised the question yesterday, may I say that I did so only to have the rules clarified. I too am satisfied with your ruling.

REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT BY CHAIRMAN OF WARTIME PRICES AND TRADE BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I crave your indulgence and the indulgence of the house to rise on a question of privilege which affects the rights of every member of this house.
In the press of yesterday and this morning appears a press release by Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, which reads in part as follows:

Asked to comment on allegations that the wartime prices and trade board used gestapo methods in the course of its enforcement activities, Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, stated bluntly to-day that such statements were utter nonsense.
Further he stated:
On the other hand we have this type of wild accusation about gestapo procedure.
Further he stated:
I resent strongly the use of the word "gestapo" and I do not propose to let it pass without expressing my objection to such loose and improper language.
These remarks by Mr. Gordon refer to a speech made by myself in this house on May 21, reported at- page 1726 of Hansard. The press statement adds:
Mr. Gordon was commenting on remarks made in the Commons last night by G. S. White, Profressive Conservative member for Hastings-'eterborough.
We in this chamber, Mr. Slpeaker, are members of parliament sent here by the people to represent them. In the discharge of this high duty the most valuable right which we possess is our freedom of speech in debate. It is a right which we must ever be jealous to guard ; for it is the foundation of our effectiveness as members here. Its fundamental importance is recognized in the immunity which we are given from legal action for any statement made in this chamber. I must submit, sir, that our independence in this chamber should include complete freedom from attack, abuse or censure from any paid public official whom we may happen to mention in the course of our duties in debate here. I construe Mr. Gordon's statement as an admonition to me, a representative of the people, that I must not again in the terms I use or in any other way express my views of his administration in terms objectionable to himself.
. I resent any such admonition or any attempt by Mr. Gordon to dictate the language to be used in this chamber. I regard it as high impertinence and an insolence directed against every member of this house. The proper, person to answer any attack made upon anjf branch of the public service in this house is the responsible minister. It will be a most serious thing if the time ever comes when a member of parliament before criticizing a branch of the public service, must first consider the abuse which he may draw down upon himself from the officials of that service.
I have no intention, Mr. Speaker, of being instructed or lectured in any way by Mr. Gordon, a public servant. The remarks made by Mr. Gordon are simply a further indication of the gestapo methods of the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board in attempting

Railways and Shipping
to castigate a member of parliament. The language I used was neither loose nor improper, but accurately and justly described the actions of the officials who operate under the direction of Mr. Gordon. Apparently Mr. Gordon is above the government and the minister who administers the department under which the board is placed.

speechtext: Is the Minister of National Defence yet in a position to make a statement regarding the retention of Aldershot military camp for permanent force training for the army?

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: ALDERSHOT MILITARY CAMP-JUNIOR PERMANENT FORCE OFFICERS
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for asking the question. I have had similar
Army-Aldershot Camp

inquiries and representations from the Minister of Finance, the senior member for Halifax, and, I believe, most if not all of the Nova Scotia members and senators with respect to the future of Aldershot camp. The question arose, I believe, in consequence of some press dispatch, which I did not see, to the effect that training of the permanent force was to be centralized in Ontario or Manitoba. That is not accurate. The active force will include the brigade group, field units, training schools and establishments, the usual static units at district headquarters, and so on. These are to be spread across Canada. I do not recall how many schools there are, but there are several of them. One will be located at Dartmouth, Nova Scotia-an artillery school; and others will be located right across Canada: one in British Columbia, some in the prairies, some in Ontario and, I believe, in Quebec. Aider-shot camp was not used before the war as a permanent establishment where troops were quartered the year round. It will not be so used after the war. In that respect it will be in the same position as Petawawa, Ipperwash, Dundurn, Farnham, Utopia and a number of others. These camps will be used in the summer months for the training of the reserve army, and no doubt a skeleton staff will be kept there the year round. So far as the permanent force units are concerned, they will be located where there are permanent quarters. Before the war in Nova Scotia that was and will continue to be Halifax and Dartmouth.
After receiving notice of this question from several hon. members I went into the matter rather carefully. I found that the total permanent force strength in military district No. 6, Nova Scotia, will be in the vicinity of 1,200 men as against about 500 before the war. The same plan will be followed there as throughout the rest of Canada. Aldershot is to-day and will continue to be the principal training centre for the reserve army in Nova Scotia.

speechtext:
When the house rose last evening I was endeavouring to point out that this group have been carrying on this debate in the hope of getting a better deal for the farmers and the workers of this country. I also invited the private members who support the government to give us their opinion as to whether or not they approve the actions of the government in relation to its price ceiling policy up to the present.
In the short time remaining at my disposal I should like to put a few constructive proposals before the government and the house, in order to establish that we are not here merely to criticize, although we do not pull any punches when criticism is necessary, but also to propose steps to the government and to the house which we feel would be for the benefit of the people. I have five points which I should like to place on the record by way of indicating a certain line of action which in my opinion will meet with the approval of the great majority of the people of Canada.
My first point is that the government should permit increases in the prices of farm products and fish in relation to the cost of production. In view of the action of the wartime prices and trade board, authorized by the government, in permitting certain increases in the prices of manufactured articles-I do not need to go through the very long list of articles concerned-I do not think anyone in this house will deny that it is now necessary to give consideration to an increase in the prices of certain farm products and fish.
My second point is that the government should permit an immediate increase in all substandard wages. While in some instances wages went up during the war, wages in many other occupations are far below the standard, and there is necessity for an immediate increase in these, wages in order that the people concerned may make both ends meet.
The third point I suggest is that a floor price of $1.55 per bushel be placed under wheat for the next five years, with comparable floors under other farm products, fish, and wages. There has been a great deal of talk in this house over the contention that the ceiling on wheat should be raised. While I believe that is true to a certain extent, what the farmer wants and needs for the next five years is not so much a ceiling pegged at a high level but some certainty as to what is going to be the floor price. At the present time provision is made for a floor price of $1 per bushel for the next five years. If the present trend is to continue, the cost of production will be such that $1 per bushel simply will not be sufficient, so I think the government should not hesitate to increase the floor price to the figure I have mentioned, in view of the world situation, the possibilities of markets, and the prices of other articles.
My fourth proposal is that the government increase the income tax exemption to $2,000 for married persons and $1,200 for single persons. My reason for offering this proposal is obvious from what has gone before. The purchasing dollar to-day does not buy what the purchasing dollar bought two years ago. A single person with an income of $1,000 or $1,200 is not able to provide the necessities of life and at the same time pay income tax. A married man receiving $2,000 or less, with the cost of living as it is and as it seems likely to be for quite a while, certainly is not able to maintain a family and at the same time contribute by way of income tax.
My fifth proposal is that pensions to the aged and the blind be increased sufficiently to compensate for the increased cost of living. The reason for that also is obvious. This is
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

'the class of people who, as I think all hon. members will agree, have been hit hardest by the rising cost of living, because they are attempting to live-in some cases merely to exist-upon fixed incomes. They cannot go on strike and ask for higher pensions. They cannot organize and refuse to sell their produce. Evidently they cannot lobby the government with any success. Therefore it is up to the members of this house to show their appreciation for our old people who pioneered this country and made it what it is, and their consideration for the unfortunate people who are suffering from blindness and other disabilities. These people should have their pensions increased immediately in order to meet the increased cost of living.
I do not advance these proposals merely, so to speak, to put the government on the spot, but because I feel they are legitimate demands which the people of this country were led, during the last election campaign, to believe would be met. I am not going to rehash what was said at that time; I need only mention the fact that during that campaign there was a great deal of talk about the new social order. Pamphlets and other literature were printed and distributed to the people in which they were told that never again would this country go through what we experienced during the hungry thirties; never again would we suffer from lack of social security, and so on. I do not say these promises were made only by the party.now in power; every party represented in this house had such things somewhere in its programme. But it happens that the party across the way, the Liberal party, is in power at the present time, and it is the only party which can do these things for the people.
In order that; hon. members may not think I have concocted a synthetic set of proposals out of my own head, I should like to read a resolution which was submitted to me by an agricultural society at Ethelbert, Manitoba, in my constituency. The farmers who belong to this society do heavy work; they are not the sort of farmers someone to my right mentioned the other day, who work six months a year and spend the other six months in California. I am sure not one member of this society has ever seen Florida or California, or ever hopes to do so. Here is what they say:
Whereas the members of the Ethelbert agricultural society have always been in favour of stabilization of prices of farm produce at a fair price to the producer, provided that the things the farmer has to buy are kept at a reasonable price.
Whereas the prices of many commodities the farmers have to buy have risen considerably, and the prices of farm products have not increased correspondingly.
It is therefore resolved that this society go on record as:

1.	Deploring the action of the dominion government in allowing an increase in the price of farm implements;
2.	Recommending that the dominion government reconsider its decision to permit an increase in the price of farm machinery, or take immediate steps for a general increase of all farm products corresponding to the increased cost of production.
I could go on and quote resolutions of the same sort from other farm organizations and labour unions, in which they point out that if they are to be asked to help maintain the price stabilization policies of this country, in return they have a right to expect some security and fairness of treatment; in other words that the load will not be placed upon the low income groups of this country. That is the stand we take on this side of the house. I believe this debate has brought out what I said in my opening remarks yesterday;, that is, that if the government had taken this house into its confidence; if it had brought before the house this question of raising price ceilings and making certain unannounced adjustments, giving the members of this house an opportunity to express their opinions and give their advice in good faith, it could have saved itself a great deal of trouble and could have won the respect and support of the great majority of the people of this country. As it is to-day the government have sowed seeds of distrust in the minds of the people. To-day no one in the country feels secure, because they believe the whole price control structure is built upon sand, so to speak, which may be washed away at any time. I think it is high time the government did something to restore the faith of the people of this country in the principles of fairness in connection with price controls.

I am not satisfied to stop there. 1 am dissatisfied with the price ceilings on the products of the farms to-day, as are a great many farmers at this particular time. May I emphasize that in that sub-amen.dment the group to my left approves these conditions in connection with price ceilings to-day. By the wording of the subamendment. it would seem that they are satisfied with the recent increase in the price of gasoline in the prairie provinces, and with many other grievances; because they have taken the meat out of that original amendment and pinned their whole grievance to the increase in the price of farm implements, rightly oj- wrongly, after all that has taken place by way of protestations of various members to my left. I think we have to be careful about the wording of that upon which we are going to vote, despite protestations Which are raised in the house.
So I say there are these many grievances which are bound to aggravate the situation from the point of view of agricultural production. I say distinctly that I for one am dissatisfied with the .price of wheat to-day,
with the price of beef, the price of hogs and of dairy products, as compared with the prices in any other of the united nations with which we were associated in the prosecution of the war.
As was so ably said by the hon. member for Lake Centre yesterday, great famines prevail in many parts of the world. We know little in Canada about the cost of this war- certainly not in the lack of foodstuffs. But lightly or wrongly, with the war over, many of these farmers are letting up on their production.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) from my own province seemed to be quite satisfied with the plight of the farmers to-day. I know that he did not speak even for all the farmers in his own constituency, let alone for the province of Manitoba.
Recently the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, through their executive, asked the dominion government to make an adequate study of farm costs of production at the earliest possible day and to relate the findings to the incomes of other Canadians. The federation suggested that the study should be made with all speed, and they added:
Agricultural prices cannot be fixed equitably, during the period in which they must be fixed, until the essential facts are known. Agricultural production cannot be increased unless the prices of farm products are reasonable in relation to costs and earnings of non-farmers . . . The simple quick way to achieve parity between farm and city workers is to permit farm prices to rise until the scales are balanced. Those who know something about farm earnings and incomes will agree that an immediate 50 per cent increase in tarm prices would be necessary to bring farm hours into line with city hours.
Just the other evening, when my colleague the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) was speaking, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) asked what "parity" is. I have heard him ask that many times. The minister did take a basis for organized labour, namely the years 1926-29, as parity. It is recognized throughout this country, of course, that there is considerable difference of opinion between the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture. I think it is conceded by those who follow current events that they do not see eye to eye. They are even far apart in some cases. But surely there should be agreement between the ministers and their parliamentary assistants. When we were debating this subject of parity on September 25, during the last session, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) rose in his place and spoke for forty minutes on the. subject, in an endeavour to point out that this governement was fighting to get the principle of parity prices

Stratton was convicted a short time ago for offering to sell a used McLaughlin-Buick car for more than the ceiling price. He pleaded guilty and so there was no evidence given, but we believe that he advertised the car for sale for approximately the ceiling price and when a buyer came he quoted the man $1,300. The man wanted to buy, even at $1,300, but Stratton did not sell it to him. The chap was a Brandon man and later phoned long distance to Stratton and Stratton, who claims he did not want to sell to this fellow at all, told the man over the phone that the car was already sold for $1,275. This was not true, as Stratton apparently had not sold the car at all.
, So far as the writer can gather, this would-be purchaser then got in touch with the Brandon wartime prices and trade board with the result that Stratton was contacted by the wartime prices and trade board officials and the Mounted Police. He told them what had happened, signed a statement, came down to Portage, his ear was immediately seized at Portage la Prairie and he was left to get home the best way he could. The writer was retained and the writer immediately drew an assurance that Stratton would not dispose of the car above the ceiling price and sent it to Mr. Siddall, representative of the wartime prices and trade board in Winnipeg.
When the case came up for trial, which was a week after the seizure of the car, my client pleaded guilty and w-as fined $50 and costs. The wartime prices officials did not think this was enough. After the plea of guilty, counsel for the wartime prices and trade board asked the magistrate to make an order to further retain the car. The writer naturally took the stand that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to do so. As a matter of fact, we thought it was unlawful for them to have retained the car for the week preceding the case. The magistrate refused to make the order and the car was turned over to Stratton.
We now have the spectacle of this ear being seized under an order signed by C. H. Blair, assistant secretary, presumably, of the wartime prices and trade board. We enclose herewith a copy of this warrant. The car has been tied up so far in Stratton's own garage, but, as you can see, the board apparently are going to sell this car notwithstanding the fact that Stratton does not want to sell it and notwithstanding the fact that he has given an assurance that he will not peddle it above the ceiling price.
We have made application to Mr. John C. Ross of Winnipeg for re-consideration of this matter and have asked him to refer it to Ottawa. We are writing you to ask you now if you would be good enough to intercede in this matter and see if he can have his ear released, as he needs it in his oil business.

The regulation under which this has been seized reads as follows:
"16. Any goods which any person buys or sells or in any way deals with or attempts to buy or sell or in any way deal with contrary to these regulations may (in addition to any other penalty which may have been imposed on any person or to which any person may be subject, with relation to such unlawful act or omission, and whether or not any prosecution in relation thereto has been commenced) be seized and detained and shall be liable to forfeiture at the instance of the Minister of Justice upon proceedings in the Exchequer Court of Canada or in any superior court, sub-'ject, however, to a right of compensation on the part of any innocent person interested in such property at the time it became liable to forfeiture or who acquired an interest therein subsequent to such time as a bona fide transferee for value without notice, w-hich right may be enforced in the same manner as any other right against His Majesty."
That, I think, is a pretty high-handed exercise of authority, and the assurances we have had in other matters with regard to the rights and liberties of the individual citizen are certainly ignored in that order. It shows there is need in this country to-day for the bill of rights which was debated here a short time ago. The letter continues:
Whether the regulation will hold water, or not, is beside the point, as people like Stratton have not money to fight these various bureaus of the- government, but for a free country this is pretty drastic procedure when officials of the government without any court order whatsoever can walk into a man's place and tell him that they are going to seize and sell his own property.

Mr. Speaker, the house has listened to a very interesting debate, precipitated by the amendment moved by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bracken). After a careful study of the amendment and of the amendment to the amendment I think we can all agree that there are two main issues before the house with which we ought to be particularly concerned. The first issue is directly contained in the wording of the amendment, which states that because of the government price ceiling policy, agricultural production is being hampered. The second issue is not stated in the wording of the amendment, but I think the speeches of practically every hon. member to my right have been to the effect that price controls in this country ought to be abolished.
I have listened carefully to every debate which has taken place in this house, both in this session and in the last, and they have left with me the impression up to the present time that the Conservative party is un-
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

equivocally opposed to the price control system which was established in Canada during the war years.
This is a very important subject. It is not only of importance to the farmers; it is of great importance to the workers, including the industrial and the white-collar workers, and I think every party in this house should have its leader go on record as to what is to be the policy of that party with respect to price control. Our leader has already gone on record with respect to that situation. I have not yet heard what is the official stand of the Progressive Conservative party in this matter, and I should like to know what it is.
With respect to the first issue, I do not think there is any question but that the government's policy with respect to price ceilings is hampering agricultural production. I am in favour of maintaining the price control system which was built up in this country during the war years. I support the maintenance of it because I happen to have had the privilege of being in another British country during the war years where price control was not in effect. I can tell the members of this house that the people in that country suffered considerably because of the fact that there was no control over the prices of goods. I refer to Newfoundland. In St. John's, Newfoundland, in 1942 a dozen eggs cost $1.20-I know, because I was there-and other agricultural products were just as high. Coal sold at $25 a ton in St. John's because there was no control over prices. While I do not agree with the economic policies put forward by the present government, I do feel that we ought to give them credit for building up in this country an effective system of price control. The only objection I have to that policy up to the present time is that they are allowing private interests to punch holes in the price system, and I venture to say that we may come to the time when we shall have to abandon price controls owing to the fact that we have allowed the system to become honeycombed by rising prices.
This is the position of the farmer as far as I can see it. Under our price control system we have permitted the prices of a large number of goods to be increased, and on some of our commodities we have permitted the price control to be completely lifted. That has resulted in a reduction in the purchasing power of Canadian farmers, because the prices of goods they have to buy have gone up steadily ever since the beginning of this year. The increase in the price of gasoline, petroleum products, farm machinery, clothing

and a great number of other commodities has reduced the purchasing power of the farming group as a whole.
But what applies to the farmer applies also to the labourer. I have listened with great interest to hon. gentlemen to my right discussing the subject, and they have tried to tell us that the farmers and the labourers of the country cannot unite on a common policy because their interests are divergent. This is not true. The farmers and the .industrial workers are in the same boat; the economic problems that confront the one group equally confront the other; and it is up to us to see that we follow some policy that will be favourable to both these groups.
I would like to put on the record an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of May 17 dealing with the increase in the cost of living to the industrial workers of the country. It comes from George Burt, Canadian director of United Automobile Workers of America, and this statement appears:
Instead of wages rising since the end of the war, they have been falling. A.verage hourly rates in money terms are down at least three per cent, real hourly rates are down nearly six per cent. Average weekly earnings dropped ten per cent and real weekly earnings, take-home pay, dropped thirteen to fourteen per cent. Mr. Burt made this announcement as the dominion bureau of statistics reported that the cost of living index had reached 120-8 as of April 1, the highest point since the war.
He goes on to say that a great many authorities in Canada have stated that if we ,are to increase the wages of the industrial workers we must of necessity increase all other costs of materials in this country, and he points out that this is not the situation. He refers to what an increase in pay would mean to the cost of production of agricultural implements. This is for the United States:
In the United States a three-bottom gang plough, for which the farmers pay $153,50, has a manufacturing labour cost of only $11.17, while a cream separator, which costs $100.84 and which bears the highest labour cost of any agricultural implement, requires a wage bill of only $14.66. In the case of cream separators, therefore, a thirty per cent increase in wages, with no improvement in labour productivity, would raise unit costs by only four per cent.
Recently I saw an interesting article in one of the western newspapers. It dealt with the increased productivity of Canadian industry in the war years, from a survey made by the war production board, which stated that in 3,750 of our largest industries, comprising forty-two different companies, the productive efficiency, when they shall have been reconverted to peace-time conditions by July 1, will have increased by some 86 per cent over

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
1939. But the additional amount of labour employed will be only 33 per cent. Reducing these two factors to equal terms, when these plants are reconverted to peace-time conditions their productive efficiency will have increased since 1939 approximately 40 per cent. That means that they will be able to make the same production with approximately 40 per cent less labour. This is not true for the whole Canadian industrial picture, but it is true for that number of industries. The only possible way in which to meet the situation is to reduce hours of labour and maintain the same rates of pay.
In order to show the effect which removal of price ceilings has had throughout the country, I should like to quote from a resolution I received from the federal union of base metal workers, No. 172, at Flin Flon, Manitoba:
Federal local No. 172. which speaks for the great majority of the workers in this community, is making strong representations to the federal government to take action to forestall the deplorable situation that is fast developing in this community. With the allowance of certain price increases and the lifting of ceilings on other products and services, we are rapidly approaching a condition where the pay envelope no longer contains sufficient buying power to meet our daily needs. We appreciate the difficulties that are being encountered in the reconversion period but feel that the workers here are being asked to bear more than their share of the burden.
That is the general opinion abroad through^ out the country. The workers of Canada are of the opinion that the government is removing price ceilings at this time, or revising them upward because of pressure that is being brought to bear by groups in the country. That pressure is being brought to bear by large industries in Canada who are anxious to make a killing on the vast backlog of production that exists in the country,,and I do not think the government of the day should yield to it. They should have stood firm and refused to grant many of these increases.
I do not want to go on record as being opposed to adjusting the price system. It may be necessary in certain instances to increase or decrease prices, but I think it should be done scientifically and should not be done until it has been thoroughly proven that the increases are necessary. If the prices of the commodities which the farmer has to buy are to be increased by increasing the price ceiling, then we must of necessity increase the selling price of his commodity, so that his buying power will remain substantially the same.
I should like to refer to a few remarks that have been made during the course of this debate by hon. gentlemen to my right. The other evening I listened with a great deal of
interest to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) as he spoke on this subject. He spoke at great length and with great force, but in all fairness I do not think that he dealt with the subject in the manner in which he should have. For instance, one of his statements was, "As a friend of labour I take second place to no one." I presume he was referring to the group as a friend of labour. I do not think the actions of the Progressive Conservative party have proven that. Their actions did not prove that from 1930 to 1935, and I do not believe they prove it to-day. It will be remembered by all hon. members what the leader of the Conservative party had to say on this subject in 1933, when there was a great deal of labour unrest throughout the country. He said that it would be necessary for the government of that day to apply the iron heel of ruthlessness when dealing with the situation. That was the labour policy enunciated from 1930 to 1935. To put the word "progressive" in front of the word "Conservative" did not alter substantially the real policy of the party.
A little further on in his address the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said that the farmer was the forgotten man. That is true. It was true especially before and after the last great war and the first great war. It is fair to say that during the war the farmer received a reasonable amount of the wealth of this country. The hon member for Dufferin-Simcoe went on to tell us that this condition had existed in Canada for twenty-five years. That is also true; but do not let us forget that during part of the twenty-five years the Conservative party rvas in power. They were in power from 1930 to 1935. They had an excellent opportunity to correct the situation at that time if they had desired to do so.
In his speech this afternoon the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) made reference to remarks made by my colleague, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) who spoke in this house on this subject yesterday. He referred to remarks made by the hon. member for Dauphin concerning the speech made by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. I checked Hansard in connection with the matter, and I want to tell the house that the hon. member for Dauphin was quite right when he made that statement. I checked the original script of Hansard and I wish to quote it.

I appreciate the fact that the hon. members to my right do not wish it to get abroad that they are not in favour of extending social services; nevertheless I think we ought to keep the record straight on that issue.
We ought to consider for a few minutes what would happen in this country if we took off price controls. The results would be serious for the workers of Canada. If we were to take off the controls it is quite possible that our prices would increase by twenty-five per cent by the end of this year. This increase in price would take place on all agricultural and industrial commodities. If that happened we would have a spiral of inflation with which agriculture would not catch up for the next three or four years. An agricultural depression would hit this country, and it would require five or six years to get back to normal. Possibly we would not get back to normal until different policies were followed. In this regard I should like to quote what United States authorities have to say with respect to price control. I shall quote from a statement made by Mr. Paul Porter, administrator of the OPA in the United States. This statement was made before the banking and currency committee on April 17, 1946. Speaking of the possibility of the lifting of price controls in the United States Mr. Porter said:
We cannot assume that the boom would collapse in a single year as it did last time. The rise in prices might well continue. As they moved up to levels 75 and 100 per cent above current prices, the purchasing power of the dollars that American families have put into war bonds, insurance policies and other forms of savings would continue to fall. If present prices doubled, the things which a dollar bought on September 1, 1939, would cost $2.60. To put it another way, the dollar's 1939 purchasing power would have shrunk to 38 cents.	.

If we are to follow a similar course in this country it is only natural to expect that we shall get a similar result, and I wish to go on record as being in favour of retaining price controls, with the proviso that as the situation develops the price of agricultural products ought to be/raised in line with the price control system of maintaining the purchasing power of the farmers of Canada.

I had not intended taking" part in this debate, but it has gone on for so many days that I wish to put myself on record as being solidly behind the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Ilsley) in his endeavour to maintain price controls.
I have listened to the debates, and I have listened with great interest to what the western members hare said. I am particularly concerned with what affects primary producere, and more /particularly fishermen. I am sympathetic to the problems of the westerners, and I trust that we shall get their consideration in matters that affect the people of the maritimes and" the Pacific, the fishing constituencies of the inland lakes and all across Canada. It seems to me that undue stress has been put upon the position of the farmers. I would suggest, in a very kindly way, that the farmers will get more sympathy if they do not emphasize only their own case and make themselves out to be the people wdio are alw'ays abused, because I do not think that is the case. I am sympathetic toward the -farmers; I have many of them in my constituency but, as I said, I am even more sympathetic toward the fishermen.
As far as price control is concerned, having lived in European countries where I have seen the black market work; having listened to various arguments from the opposite side of the house which are to some extent conflicting, I should say we are fortunate in having our present set-up with the wwtime prices and trade board which at least knows where it is going and what it is doing, and I hope we shall retain it for quite some time. I w-ould

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
not want anyone to think I should like to see prices remain as they are now, for all time. That would be a stupid statement to make. When supply equals demand it seems to me only common sense that we shall be able to relinquish certain price controls. At the present time you do not have to go out and sell articles; you must-go to the seller and ask if you may buy them. When the time comes that people have to go out and sell things, then some controls may be removed. There may be times when you will have to allow price ceilings to rise in order to increase production, as has been done in connection with farm machinery. I am not an industrialist, but the industrialist is a human being like anyone else, and iit seems only reasonable that he should be able to get a fair return for his efforts or for the money he has invested, just as the farmer or anyone else should.
I have only one suggestion to offer. I own a few shares of stock in a company which produces farm equipment. I would not sell those shares now, because they are very much lower than the price at which I bought them many years ago. I suggest to hon. members on the opposite side of the house that if they believe these companies are going to make so much money and are going to do so well, they should either individually or in groups buy up this stock. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. I do not want to go in with them, because I do not feel like putting money into farm equipment stock at the present time. I do not believe there is much profit in it, but that is my suggestion. When some of them come back here and tell me they or their organizations hare done so, then I think they will have a little more to talk about.
I hope that eventually our price control organization and many other bureaux will be done away with, so that we may get back to where we were before the war. But we must be very careful in going about this. I suggest that it takes a man of courage to maintain these price controls and continue the policy that has been adopted by the wartime prices and trade board. It would be very easy for the Acting Prime Minister to say, "Oh, yes; we will relinquish this control and that control." It is so easy to say yes, but it is a little different when you have to say no, with perhaps some of your own constituents fighting against you and some people over the whole country opposing you. I like a man who can say no when he believes that is the right thing to do. Regardless of what happens in this House of Commons, I will leave it to the public to decide who is
right and who is wrong. I am supporting the Acting Prime Minister and the wartime prices and trade board, hoping that, as time goes on, certain controls may be dropped, and that we shall continue to receive popular support until such time as we can do away with 'all these things.

A few days ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made the statement that the farmers of this country were happier-I think that was the word he used-than they had been for many years. I believe he was right up to a few weeks ago, but judging from the letters I am receiving now the farmers are not satisfied. What is the situation in Canada to-day? A great many people are dissatisfied. The workers are dissatisfied with their wages. The farmers are dissatisfied with the removal of the milk subsidy, for example. We have a strike in the logging industry, and we are threatened with other strikes all over Canada. According to the newspapers we are threatened with a strike of farmers right here in the province of Ontario. These farmers threaten to throw their milk down the drain. I do not like strikes; I think they should be avoided, if at all possible. I do not like them because those who do the striking are in the long run, the losers. In respect of wages, if they get increases under the present system, immediately the cost of the article made from their labour goes up, and the increase in the wage they obtain through striking is counteracted by the cost of the article they must buy.
The farmer has no protection; he is not in a position to strike. Perhaps the milk producers could throw their milk down the drain for a few days or a few weeks, but who wants to see that? Little children will suffer if a thing like that is done. We do not want to see children going without milk in this country for a month, while the farmers are throwing milk down the drain.
I heard over the radio last night that the government was going to have a meeting to consider putting the subsidy back on rmll-I hope something will be done. However, I did make the statement in the house last year, in my maiden speech, that I did not believe the government would do the things that would have to be done in order to get the things the people of this country want. Those things are security, stabilized prices for farmers. and wages for workers in industry which

will give them a decent standard of living. We want them to know they are going to have jobs all the time, and not just some of the time.
I have been listening to some of the statements made in the house, and have been surprised at some of them. The hon. member who has just taken his seat comes from a different part of the country. Then Tuesday evening the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) told us injustices were being suffered by the fishermen on the east coast. I support the fishermen, or any other group of men who work for their living; because we must realize some day, sooner or later, that wealth is produced by the people who work, and that the working class, the people who have produced the wealth of this country in the last hundred years, to a large extent have been poverty stricken.
I was surprised when the hon. member for Charlotte said this:
Sticks that are driven into the ground are anywhere from 20 feet to 60 feet in length. In 1940 I could buy a 50-foot stick for $3.50. In 1946 they are $12.50 each.
Here is an instance of a great increase in the price of something the fishermen has to buy. Where I come from, if a member for my constituency did not rise in his place in the house and protest against that sort of thing, he would not be a member very long. I am surprised that the hon. member for Charlotte did not protest on Tuesday evening when he was speaking.
Then, speaking again about the fishermen, he said:
They are standing on their own feet and not asking for help. They will not ask for help as long as they can make a living, and they are ready to work for it.
Then he went on to say:
In the winter time I have been twenty miles off shore, taking sardines on board a boat....
And so on. He proceeded to tell how hard he had to work. I realize he had to work hard for a living, and I am trying to represent people who have to work hard for a living. I want to see people who have to work as hard as the hon. member worked get something for the wealth they have produced.
On Tuesday evening we heard a speech from the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). This is what he said as reported at page 1744 of Hansard:
I speak as a member of the party that is recognized in Canada to-day as being the farmers' party.

You bet your life, it is the farmer and the working man who suffers most when deflation comes.
Do we want deflation? We do not. As our leader has said in this debate, we do not want high prices one day and low prices the next. What we are trying to make the house see is that we want stabilized prices, so that the farmer will know what he is going to get when he puts in a crop, so that the working man will know what his wages are going to be, and will not be losing his job.
What happens when we have deflation? We went through a period of deflation after the first great war and before the second one. I have given reasons before in the house why we have had those periods of deflation. I have been satisfied for some time that if we continue under the capitalistic system we shall have those inflationary and deflationary periods; there is no way out of it. If, as the hon. member has said, his party is in favour of taking the ceilings off farm products, he must also be in favour of taking the ceilings off every other product. That is not what the farmers of Canada want to-day, and that is not the kind of party they want to represent them.
Later in his speech the hon. member said:
Competition, reasonable pay for services, recompense for individual effort, choice of vocation-all these things are influenced by the law of supply and demand.
Economists used to tell us that two great laws regulated our economic system, the law of competition and the law of supply and demand. There was a time when those two great natural economic laws did work, but nobody can tell me that they are working to-day or that they have worked in the last twenty years. Is there competition in this country as between one big business and another? Absolutely none. There is a certain amount of competition among small business men but there is no competition and has not been for some time between the large industries in this country. We had proof of that when Mr. Duncan, manager of the Massey-Harris Company, was before the 1937 committee of this house on farm machinery prices. He was asked, "How do you arrive at prices? Do you all get together and fix prices?" He said, "No, we wait until International Harvester brings out their price list and then we bring one out like it." There is competition in this country among labourers for jobs when there are five labourers for every job, but there is no competition so far as big business is concerned.
As to the law of supply and demand, I think many of us in this house know something of that law. There are two kinds of demand.

Pme Ceiling-Farm Products

There is what we call the effective demand. Then there is another demand which many of us know more about, namely, the stomach demand. There was a stomach demand all through the 1930's, when people did not have the money to buy what they needed, and so that demand was not effective. Does anybody want to go back to the old competitive system and the law of supply and demand? I am a cooperator. I believe in cooperation. I believe that competition is just as bad among business as it is between nations. Competition is one of the things that is responsible for war and for a great deal of the hardships that we have seen in this country. Take the small business man, for instance, who has worked hard, saved a little money and established a small business. Then, under the competitive system somebody comes along and sets up a store beside him, perhaps someone with a little more capital, better stock or connected with a chain store, or it might be a large corporation. What happens to the small business man? We know by government statistics that thousands of small businesses go out of existence or go bankrupt year after year. Do we want to return to that system? That is not what the farmers are going to support.

Mr. Speaker, many speakers in this debate have presented statistics to prove their case that the government's recent policy of decontrol has meant undue hardship for agricultural producers and workers in this country. I believe, and I think in this I am in complete agreement with all members of this group, that this whole problem of decontrol facing the government to-day stems out of the lack of policies which they should have formulated during the war. If those policies had been formulated we would have known when we entered this post-war period exactly where we were going. I am sure that this government has no policy in regard to decontrol. It is giving in to pressure behind the scenes.
As a new member of this house, I would have thought this government would have learned something during the war, but I am quite sure now that we have simply the same set-up that we had during the war, a set-up for the protection of the vested interests of this country. In any proper policy of decontrol you cannot treat agriculture independently of other branches of our Canadian economy. We must recognize that our whole economy is so interlinked that farmers and workers and all the Canadian people are interdependent. But once again we see the government giving in to these powerful corporations who, behind the scenes, are exerting pressure upon it.

During the war these companies made tremendous profits. I do not wish to give figures that have already appeared on Hansard but will say briefly that in 600 odd companies listed here the profits ranged from 13-3 to 17-6 per cent. These companies have made money and they are making money again. It is true, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated, that agriculture had some of the best years it ever had during the war; nevertheless he went on to state that the average income of agriculture in its best years was only $2,000 par farm.
I should like to say a word about our national debt. On March 31, 1939, our gross debt, according to the bureau of statistics, was $3,710,610,592.87, and in 1945 it had grown to 815,712,181,527.26. This means that once again the people who made profits in the past during the development of this country are in a preferred position, with the taxpapers of this country owing money to them.
When we are planning for the post-war period we should predicate our whole policy on making available to the common people of this country the things which they produce. In 1939 we had a national income of $3 billion and that has grown to-day to a national income of $9 billion. Our whole system should be so arranged that the workers will be enabled to get a fair share of the things that agriculture produces and that the farmers will be able to buy the things they need which the industrial workers produce. Look at the number of our farms to-day that have no bathtubs and no modern bathroom equipment; at the number that are without cars and all the amenities of life that they should and could have. But the decontrol policy of this government is bringing about a situation that lowers the purchasing power of farmers so that they will be unable to buy what the industrial workers produce. Consequently vre are going to pass through another phase of unemployment.
It seems to me that the machinery companies in their pressure on this government are doing very much what the aluminum company did in the months just before the war, when they refused to go into production until they got the profits which they demanded. Tremendous profits have been made by these big companies. The Shipshaw power project during 1941 to 1945 received from the government a special depreciation amounting to $164 million, in addition to huge profits based on prices of from fifteen to seventeen cents per pound. The machine companies are also making huge profits. What the government is doing by making this gap in the ceiling on farm machinery will result in breaking the

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
ceiling on every other commodity. I have here a report from the Free Press Prairie Farmer of May 7, 1946, headed "Farm hardware price rise seen", in which one hardware merchant who specializes in hardware materials which farmers require says that price increases of from 5 to 10 per cent on farm hardware can be expected.
There was an example of this to hand yesterday in statutory orders and regulations, May 1, 1946, by this government providing that prices of metal beds, cribs and bassinettes are increased by 10 per cent and metal bed-springs, trunks and cots are going up 12} per cent. So that in fact we have no longer any control policy.
As reported at page 1781 of Hansard the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) in his speech the other day said, referring to the leader of this gronp:
....the C.C.F. party supports the government in its stand that there shall be no increase in the prices of farm products in this country.
I believe that when the leader of our group speaks he will make it abundantly clear that he never said that and does not believe in it, neither does any member of this group. We have always taken the stand that we believe in a scientific, organized Canadian economy whereby the price of farm products will bear a fair relationship to the cost of their production. But what is happening at this time? Let us consider the serious position of our 800,000 veterans, most of whom have come back only to find that the government has allowed the cost of housing to go up about 50 per cent, the cost of machinery to rise by 12} per cent, with increases in other directions. These boys and girls returning to civilian life find that their gratuities are insufficient to buy or build houses or to buy farm machinery; yet their incomes are stabilized. In consequence, they are not able to rehabilitate themselves. This is not fair, because these young people went into the services with the idea that they would not be any worse off when they came back than those who did not enlist. They find that through conditions beyond their control housing costs have gone up 50 per cent, and by a statutory order issued on May 20 the government has allowed the price of furniture to be increased from 10 to 12} per cent. So it looks as though the government in its decontrol policy has no regard for these people. The outlook is seYious.
What we need is, not a plan for agriculture alone or for the industrial worker alone, but general planning on a basis whereby our Canadian economy can be scientifically arranged so that the people of Canada can 63260-115}
absorb the goods which they produce. I do not think it is sensible to look for foreign markets so long as the people on the farms are without radios, bathroom equipment and other necessities. Likewise I do not believe that, apart from the emergency we are facing to-day, we need to worry about foreign, markets for our agricultural products. As was pointed out the other day, when we went into war and began to put pay cheques into the pockets of our workers they started to buy the beef, butter, pork and cheese which the farmers were producing, and the Minister of Agriculture himself said, when speaking in the province of Saskatchewan, not much beef had been shipped out until we had to resort to the rationing of beef. The point was that for the first time in .many years purchasing power was put into the pockets of large numbers of people.
What is happening to-day? It would seem that the same situation is likely to recur which existed prior to 1939, when the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and Mr. Douglas, now Premier of Saskatchewan, proposed on various occasions that money be provided to put to work the young men who were then on relief. The question arose then which we hear now, where is the money to come from? I suggest that it will not be many 'months before we shall have the same situation. The money will be in the hands of the financial corporations of this country, and we shall again be faced with the same inquiry, as to where the money is to come from. Yet we have the farmers needing equipment, because for six years prior to the war, owing to low prices, they did not have purchasing power, and in the six years following, because steel was needed for war purposes, they were and are, though provided with some purchasing power, unable to replace their farm machinery. While we pay much lip-service to all-out food production we are in fact achieving nothing of the kind because of these restrictions. I know in my district people are wondering if it is worth while trying to farm, and certainly the young men and women returning from the war are not going back to the farms.
I do not think I need speak any longer on this matter, but in conclusion I charge the government with failure in its decontrol policy, on five counts.
In the first place, it has failed to maintain full production in the industrial field, because it is not providing incentives.
In the second place, it has failed to maintain all-out food production because of its income
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

tax policy, the increase, of three cents per gallon on gasoline, and the increased costs of farm machinery.
In the third place, it has failed to achieve full employment. I have just inquired of the bureau of statistics as to the number of registered unemployed in Canada, and I wish to point out that at this time, when we are supposed to go into a full housing problem and all-out food production, 225,000 persons are registered as being unable to find jobs.
In the fourth place, the government has failed to distribute the national income fairly among our people. I believe that farmers and their wives who have worked long hours during the war, and workers in industry, should be entitled to a fair share of the nation's income, that it should be so distributed as to provide decent standards of living in this country.
In the fifth place, the government has failed to maintain housing and other rehabilitation costs at levels at which the veterans can decently rehabilitate themselves.
These, Mr. Speaker, are my views on the decontrol policy. I think it is absurd for any hon. member to make suggestions or even to criticize the government merely on one phase of this policy; it must be faced as a problem of the whole Canadian economy. We in this group insist that if the country is to avert another depression, if we are to have the kind of post-war programme to which those who fought this war are entitled, it will have to be worked out on a scientific basis.
