Mr. Speaker, my reason for participating in this discussion is that for the last three decades in my own section of northern Ontario we have had the greatest agricultural development of any area in Canada. At the very outset I must state my belief that the discussion which is taking place on the resolution of non-confidence will prove beneficial to the people generally, because it will bring forcibly to the attention of parliament and of the Canadian public the controls which we have had during the war and which will probably have to be maintained to some extent for a great many years, if not for all time to come.
It is not popular to work for and to support controls, it was a real ordeal as far as I was personally concerned, because no Canadians, in fact no people living in democratic countries, relish controls even in war time, much less in peace time. However, I thought it my duty and my obligation, more particularly during the war, when I saw some dissatisfaction over rationing and price controls, to step into the breach and tell our people what these 
restrictions meant to them, to our war effort and to our allies, and I am going to do much the same thing even now that the war is over, because I know that controls are still needed.
During the present debate we have often been reminded that the war is over. It is true that the armed conflict is ended. But the war has left us a horrible and costly heritage, and I for one could never feel that after five, six or seven years of bloody conflict we could reasonably expect a heaven on earth to result. There was bound to be a residue of hardship for the Canadian people as well as for all the other peace-loving people of the world, in fact, for all the nations; and for many years to come, apart from the bloodshed, sacrifices will have to be made throughout the world so as to solve the post-war problems. It was not a pleasant thing even from the political point of view, and in this connection I wish to quote a statement made by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) in the maiden speech he delivered last year, which was so well received on all sides in the house, not only because the speech itself was an able one but because of the reputation and the ability of the hon. gentleman who delivered it:
I was in a very small shop one day located in my riding. Like most country stores it was really a tiny departmental store. In it was a dry goods section, a grocery section, a boots and shoes section, and so on. I should think one could have taken any of those departments and put it in a good-sized wheelbarrow-. The owner of that shop was somewhat annoyed on the day of my visit. It seems there had been tw-o government inspectors w-ho came to the shop during the afternoon. They travelled in very fine cars supplied with plenty of gasoline-and this was during the rationing period. One of them examined, let us say, his dry goods; the other examined, let us say, his boots and shoes, to see that all w-as in order. From my own point of view it w-as perhaps a good thing, because I think the ow-ner of the store w-as a faithful member of the Liberal party, and I left that shop with some feeling that perhaps he might change his allegiance.
This was not my own attitude in my riding. I had no desire to inquire into the political party affiliations of anyone, retailer or wholesaler, though I have no doubt that in many instances people were irritated by the controls. We all realize to-day, however, how necessary those controls were. I do not think anyone should refer to the fact that inspectors or officials of the wartime prices and trade board were travelling around in cars, good or otherwise. It is true that they did travel, but they had to travel somewhere and they had to have some means of travelling because there was a great deal of territory to be covered. It may be true that they were using

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
more gasoline than the average citizen, but I do not see any ground for criticism there, because they simply had to travel and they had to have the gasoline.
I would, however, ask hon. gentlemen this question. Have we as parliamentarians;, have we as leaders in our own individual communities, done everything which it was in our power to do to make the controls effective? It would be a very easy matter to capitalize politically against the government on the controls. It would be quite easy for me to state in this house that I am opposed to controls as such and that there should never have been any price control system. That would be popular in my section of the country. But would that be playing fair; would it be playing the game, from the point of view of the national economy? Would it be doing anything to help toward a. solution of the post-war problem?
The motion of non-confidence has been, I believe, properly analyzed and interpreted by the farmers of the country, and they will certainly not be happy about it, nor will they be inclined to commend the leader of the Progressive Conservative party and his followers for that motion, for its implications against them. The amendment carries the implication that because of the controls that have been in effect, as a necessity because of war conditions and at the present time, our farmers have not played fair and have refused to produce to the maximum of their capacity.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of this country-I think, for that matter, the same can be said of farmers everywhere-are not only a robust people, but a loyal people as well, and we know how hard they worked during the war and are still working. Unlike those engaged in industry or in the professions, they cannot draw up a chart in the spring of the year, knowing exactly how much they will grow, exactly what they will reap from the seeds they have sown, what returns they will get for the sweat of their brows. But have not all the farmers of this country, not only during the war, but under all circumstances, and under handicaps of every kind, dedicated their vocation to the good of the country as a whole, and done the best they possibly could under all conditions?
I do not believe for a moment that controls have had any effect on the farmers in the way of influencing them to curtail production or not to produce to the fullest extent possible. They have not done that in my part of the country, nor do I believe they have done it in any other section of Canada. What is more, I am positive they will not take that attitude in consequence of a slight increase
in the price of farm implements. I am speaking for the farmers and settlers in my own section at any rate.
A little later on I wish to consider, in the light of the amendment that has been proposed, prices that are actually paid in the United States, and in this connection I will quote some comments made by certain United States newspapers of wide circulation giving the reasons for prices having been so high. We all know that sometimes there is decreased production as far as farm products are concerned, but this is not due to any government policy; it is due, generally, to climatic conditions. We can be thankful that the government cannot be blamed for the weather; if the government could be blamed for it, then no government would long remain in office,, and it is really the only thing on which it can be challenged. In my part of the country in 1944 we had about one-fifth of our average hay crop, although we received some help from the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa in getting lower freight rates on hay shipped to our section. But a good many people had to sell dairy and other cattle because costs were prohibitive. The government certainly cannot be blamed for that situation.
I should like to read something that shows how pathetic the farmer's position is. It is pathetic regardless of any government policies or controls. The following is a brief article that appeared in the Regina Leader-Post in May, 1946:
There is an anxious furrow in the brows of southern Saskatchewan people as they scan the skies these days. Early though it is in the spring season, there have been several invasions already of the dreaded enemy-dust. Eyes have smarted,throats have been constricted with the acrid taste, and the wind has whipped up to the devastating proportions of ten years ago.
Few who experienced the siege of a decade ago can ever forget that period when the whole pattern of the province's economic and moral fibre rocked and reeled to a series of constant dust storms. Agriculture was, of course, the most vitally affected. Saskatchewan farmers needed and drew upon a courage almost superhuman to bolster them against the sight of constantly drifting, precious topsoil, and the knowledge that their crops and livelihood were blowing away each day with the evil drouth winds. The fact that they did stick it out grimly and steadfastly, has become yet another saga of brave Canadians. It is to be hoped they will be spared from such another trial.
Urban dwellers felt the repreeussions of the economic depression also and doctors reported that eye, ear, nose and throat trouble sprang up overnight due to the vicious onslaught of the dust-laden air.
I have read nothing that describes so poignantly the anxiety and pathos of the farmers during their seeding season as well as in the crop season. I repeat, the leader

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
of the Progressive Conservative party was ill-advised to introduce a resolution that seeks to convey to the people of the country the impression that, as a result of certain government policies, the Canadian farmers have not been true to their calling and have not produced to the best of their ability, and have seized any opportunity to curtail production.
So far as decreased acreage is concerned, I can assure the house that there will be no decrease this year as a result of the 124 per cent increase in the price of farm implements. On the contrary, there will be a larger acreage than in the past. The following Canadian press dispatch appeared early this week with reference particularly to Ontario:
Seeding of the new crops across the country is well ahead of this time last year except in the maritimes, a survey by the Canadian Press showed to-day. And farmers are planting more wheat than last year.
Winter killing of fall wheat, hay and clover crops was considerable in central and eastern Ontario. The weather so far has been unfavourable for growth of these crops and of course for pastures too, with most milking herds still stabled.
We all know this is a backward spring, and not conductive to profitable operation so far as dairying is concerned. I continue with the quotation:
Ontario is expected to seed somewhat higher acreage of spring grains, and a considerable increase in acreage of tobacco, soy beans, corn, early potatoes, field peas and sugar beets.
Surely there is no danger of defeatism in Ontario farmers and the farmers throughout Canada, no matter whait may happen to governmental activities. I continue:
Ontario expects the biggest tobacco crop in history, with a twenty per cent increase in all types. The plants will be set out around May 24. The tobacco growers are anxious for ample rainfall right now, however.
All vegetable growing districts in Ontario expect increased acreage this year in practically all vegetables. Transplanting and seeding is up to normal in most places and well ahead of normal in others.
I just wanted to put that on the record so that parliament and the people from the urban centres will know that our Canadian farmers are not discouraged. They were at times working under a great handicap. We remember the depression; we remember the terrible years of dought in the west. We have had difficult times in my own section where we have been pushing out the borders of civilization under climatic conditions that were not ideal for farming, particularly grain farming. Year after year we had to face premature frost in the fall and early frosts in the spring. In my own farming activities it was only in the seventeenth year after

seeding grain on our soil that we harvested grain crops for seed purposes. I am showing by that, that our people are not discouraged, even by the elements.
No one will make me believe that an increase in price of a fraction of one per cent will discourage all our farmers from going ahead with their work. It is a calling with them; it is a duty, besides being t'heir way of living. They have heard the appeal of the famished people of Europe; they have heard the appeal of Mr. LaGuardia, of Mr. Hoover, of the Canadian government, of every member of this parliament, of the necessity of growing more crops to feed the people of Europe. Most of them know what happened during the last war. Therefore on this score I am absolutely at ease in speaking.
I know that our farmers do not like this increase in the cost of their farm implements. They are human, the same as anyone else. I know they will never be satisfied with their lot. But that is a happy situation, because every section of our population should agitate logically, practically, sincerely and honestly for a better place in the sun, for more comfort and prosperity than they have; in a word, for a better way of life. We do not need to worry as far as the rest of our population is concerned when that takes place. The farmers are basing their opinions on that score, but they are realists. They know that today their situation is better than it was four, five or six years ago. They hope that never again will the prices that obtained during the depression be prevalent throughout Canada. At that time eggs were selling at eleven cents a dozen and butter at eighteen cents a pound. As a wholesaler and retailer I know that this was not good for Canada as a whole. It was not good for anyone. I hope that the price and floor controls which were established two years ago will, when in full swing, stabilize prices, and give a fair amount of controlled prices so far as farm production is concerned.
May I now touch on the question of price ceilings? Farmers realize that ,it cannot be absolutely rigid; it must be resilient to some extent. The same thing applies to floor prices. At times, some of the floor prices will have to be increased and decreased. Being logical, labour also knows that the workers cannot expect a rigid wage scale. Everyone knows that the industrialists cannot work or manufacture on the same prices as ten years ago, five years ago, or perhaps ten years from now. Rigidity is never conducive to the good functioning of any economic system. They have it in some countries, but surely we do not want it imposed on us. Our farmers know

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
very weill that an, increase of one-fifth of one per cent, or one^tenth of one per cent in their cost of production is not going to upset their own activities, because they have received some increases. They received an increase recently on the price of butter, and they are satisfied to some extent, but not entirely so. I know this is a delicate problem for me to deal with, but I know of no section of our population which is more logical and, practical; they understand the other viewpoint, and I know it is my duty to express my opinions on such questions forcibly and honestly.
An hon. member when speaking this afternoon said something about hon. members who had invested in farm, implement companies. I hold no brief for the farm implement companies, because the few dollars I placed in those companies had never brought me very much. I am willing to sell what, interest I have in those companies very cheaply to any member of parliament, because I have never received any dividends except some years ago,, and those small profits very likely came out of war contracts. Therefore on that score I am perfectly at ease to speak sincerely. The statements I make here I shall make to my own people, because they will be satisfied if, with a slight increase in the price of farm implements, more farm implements can be made available.
I must state frankly-I do not know how true it is-that when some farmers learned from the newspapers that farm implements were being shipped to Europe and they were not able to get them and were having a difficult time in cultivating their land, they did indulge in a certain amount of criticism. But generally speaking-and I say this sincerely- our farmers naturally accepted that increase, because they have confidence in the wartime prices and trade board and its officers, and more particularly in Mr. Gordon. He must have been a courageous and sincere man, because with his qualifications it would, have been easy for him to resign his position and get another and an easier and more lucrative one. No matter what he did, whether he increased or decreased prices, there is a section of our population who would have been willing and ready to criticize him, and sometimes unfairly. We owe him a great debt of gratitude for staying in his position not only during war time, but also at the present time. Who will challenge the statement; who will say that Mr. Gordon could not step out of his position and go into private enterprise and, because of his own initiative and ability, make more money than he makes at the present time? Personally speaking, I say that there has been some
unfair criticism levelled against him, but the vast majority of our people deeply appreciate his great accomplishments.
' With regard to price controls, I have always maintained that it is the primary duty of the department to educate our people, to make them realize the necessity of price control. After a pea-son has been fairly warned; after the organization work has been done, and the proper publicity given to the necessity of price controls, if infractions take place in these controls the law should take its course. A splendid job has been done in that connection.
I must confess that I do not claim to know all the ramifications and all the details of price control. To do so would be presumptuous on my part. I believe it was necessary during war time, and I believe it will be necessary for a number of years to come. To think in terms of ten and twenty years is to try to fool ourselves. The era of laissez-faire has gone forever, whether it is industry, farming, labour, finance, or any other occupation. The time has arrived when, for the welfare of every section of this population, the government must, of necessity, interfere to some extent with the affairs of these organizations and social groups. No matter what we may think or say-and I have no grievance against anyone who expresses his own opinions-under our present system, which I hope will be maintained indefinitely, the capitalistic system must, of necessity, revise its way in many instances in a drastic way; it must be progressive in the full sense of the word; it must realize that controls that were existing during the war will also be necessary to a limited extent -after the war is over, for the good of the whole population.
I have in my hand the report of a speech made by Mr. C. L. Burton, president of the Robert Simpson Company Limited. I have no real criticism to offer in regard to it, because he spoke as a good business man, a man who knows big industry and the questions of the big retail and wholesale houses. However, you can see in that speech how quickly he would like to see these controls done away with. I believe in these remarks he was voicing his own sentiments, as a prominent business man; but whether or not the Progressive Conservative party took .a lead from this speech, I believe the policy of that party also is to do away with controls immediately. That is often mentioned in the Conservative press; time and again on the floor of this house they come out clearly and strongly with statements that price controls should be done away with at once. I do not believe they really want price controls done away with immediately, but that
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

has a fine political ring at the present time. Any person who has been prosecuted under the law for infraction of these controls* for instance, certainly is not sympathetic toward them. But I believe that at the bottom of their hearts hon. gentlemen opposite, hope the government will continue the policy they have followed up to the present, in gradually [DOT]retreating from control but not giving it up entirely, because they know that controls are absolutely needed. I believe I am perfectly safe in making that statement. These are some of the statements by Mr. Burton:
Canada's urgent need to-day is to cut out controls and promote production.
Canada must choose-and should choose soon- in order to establish the standard of living she wrants. We have two choices:
1.	Lai'ge production and full employment; or
2.	Small output, and unemployment, due to price ceilings and wages control.
No one has yet shown that price ceilings or price controls have been or will be the cause of unemployment. Then he goes on:
Controls were universally accepted in war time. Their administration was successful during the war, having the full support of both government and business, as well as general acceptance by the public. True, the introduction and maintenance of controls were accompanied by no small measure of publicity, and various programmes of propaganda, but on the whole wartime administrators and controllers did a good job.
If they did a good job during the war, they are doing a good job at the present time, too.
It wall be generally conceded that those controls were essential which kept out of civilian use goods necessary to the forces. In any event, whatever differences of opinion there might have been during the war were subdued and submerged in the general patriotic effort against our enemies.
Now that the war is over, controls over wages and prices are on longer needed nor are they in the public interest.
In reply to Mr. Burton I would say that the public know better. To-day the public know certain safeguards are absolutely necessary, in the form of controls. In my own section of the country, about seven months ago rent control w'as lifted, and in some instances rents increased by as much as 200 per cent. The people who had been inclined to criticize rent control immediately became awmre of how necessary and how beneficial it had been to the country as a whole during war time.
Then Mr. Burton mentioned the shortage of goods, trying to tie it up with control. No businessman could make this nation believe that the shortage of goods is due to these . controls, because the controllers have studied that situation from all angles. I do not suggest that errors have not been made. I believe

the controllers have made mistakes; they are human, and they would be the first to admit it. But they have diligently rectified their mistakes. I repeat, however, that the shortage of goods .to-day is not due to price controls, though I am still puzzled as to why certain things are done in some quarters. For instance, I can go into any store in the city of Ottawa, or, for that matter, any part of Canada, and buy all the neckties I want at anywhere from fifty cents to $5.50. These ties must represent a lot of good material. On the other hand I cannot buy a man's shirt. I should like those sitting in the front row here to look into that question, because there must be some shirting material and some shirts somewhere. - If it should be found that shirts were being hoarded in order that higher prices might be obtained, then I would ask the authorities to bring those concerned immediately before the courts of this country. I make that statement deliberately, because some lines of the retail trade are absolutely famished. I do not want to impute any ulterior motive as far as industry is concerned, but I am puzzled as to why in some stores there should be all kinds of goods, goods of only limited value as far as real wear is concerned, while in the staple lines it is almost impossible to buy anything.

Yes; and something
must be wrong somewhere. I know that is where control is absolutely needed. Personally I would not go so far as to say that some traders are hoarding, but certainly there is nothing practical or logical about the situation.
It is often maintained by the official opposition during discussions in this house that our farmers should receive the same prices as United States farmers. When we deal with fiscal and national matters in this house, we are dealing with our own national economy. We do many things as well as and some of them better than they are done by our American friends, while there may be other things they do better than they are done in Canada. Would the proponents of parity prices as between United States and Canadian farmers apply the same principle all along the line and say that all production in the two countries should be on a parity ? That would be Americanism with a venegeance and would be absolutely impossible of application. Many goods are cheaper in Canada than in the United States, and vice versa. I believe our farmers realize the situation. It is only natural that they would want a higher price for their wheat when they see a higher price paid in the United States. It is only natural that they would want a higher price for their meat

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
when higher prices are paid in the United States. But, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said a few days ago, our farmers realize that this is a matter for the future as well as the present. The farmer always thinks in terms of long periods of time. When he puts the seed in the soil in the spring he knows it will be a matter of months before he gathers the fruits of his labour. The same thing applies to the public policies of the farmer. He does not look only to the immediate future; he remembers vividly when he received higher prices for his wheat after the first great war. He was not very happy under those conditions, because he knew that those prices were artificial, that they were not normal prices and that there was bound to be a reaction which would be detrimental to the wheat growers of Canada; and that was certainly what happened.
I should now like to quote from an article which appeared in Life magazine last month, dealing -with farm problems and production in the United States. I wish to make it clear that these comments relate to the United States farmer, and that I deal with this question only because it was brought forward a few weeks ago by the leader of the Progressive Conservative. party (Mr. Bracken) in asking for parity prices as far as meat and wheat were concerned. But this will show what happens in the United States, that even with the present high prices for farm products generally speaking the United States farmer is not happy. These are some of the comments:
The name of American farmer has never had a "nasty taste" before. He has been thought of rather as the backbone of our nation: as-a man who works harder, lives closer to God and nature, drinks less, raises stronger sons, votes more thoughtfully and is generally a better citizen than his urban brother. He is also thought of as getting the short end of the economic stick. But as the American businessman knows and the labour leader is learning, no stereotype is shatter-proof forever. Is it the farmer's turn to lose his reputation?
Then it goes on to explain that under war conditions the United States farmer, the same as the Canadian farmer, under a great handicap due to a shortage of labour, had so increased production that it astonished the nation and the world. These are the words:
To make all this money, and to feed our armies and allies, the American farmer increased his output during the war by over 30 per cent. He had to hump himself to do it, for the farm population (despite draft deferment and other attractions) actually declined. In fact the U.S. farmer worked like a horse from dawn to dark and nature assisted him with one of the longest spells of drought-free weather in our annals.
The next paragraph deals with climatic conditions. In the same way as did the Regina Leader, it tells the American nation the conditions under which the farmer has been working, always relying almost implicitly upon the whim of nature, and at the mercy of drought, wet weather, rain, early frost and so on. Then it continues:
The farmer whose lobbyists are among the smartest and toughest in Washington, is a political force more powerful than his numbers. But when LaGuardia began to breathe life into UXRKA and Hoover took over the famine emergency committee, fires were started both to the left and to the right of the farm politicians, leaving them nowhere to hide their naked greed. With the country at large declaring its 'willingness to be rationed and an almost scandalous glut of black-market meat, there had to be action.
Meanwhile the farm lobbies were helping congress beat the pulp out of OPA.
I want the house to remember this, that apparently the United States public is in favour of maintaining the activities of OPA. It continues:
The end of OPA would mean that grain prices would go still higher; this prospect made the farmer hold on to his grain still tighter. So to lure the grain to the dockside, government action had to take the form of a bribe.
First the farmer was offered a certificate guaranteeing him the benefit of any price increase that might occur after he sold his grain. That didn't work. Then he was offered a flat 30-cent bonus on every bushel of wheat (bringing it to $1.85) or corn (to $1.41) he sells for export before May 25. That is working a little better but not well enough. Under-Secretary of State Acheson is even talking about "seizing" the grain. At last week's official count there was twice as much wheat on the farms (some 200 million bushels) as the U.S. really needs for reserves. It is not enough to save the world, or even to fulfil our promises, but it is enough to choke the farmers who are hoarding it and damage their reputation for a long time to come.
The record of our farmers shows no hoarding; there has been no holding back, no absenteeism, if I may use that expression. No doubt they were not pleased when there was an increase in the price of gasoline. There was no rejoicing in their ranks when there was an increase in the price of farm implements, but they take these things in their stride. At the same time they know they are one of the great corner-stones of our national economy. They realize, too, that the time has arrived when, of necessity, they must more and more be recognized. These are not times when our farmers should be satisfied to be the forgotten men in our nation or in any nation.
The farmers recognize their strength. At times they have organized politically, because they have felt in their hearts at times in the past that they did not receive the attention they deserved in the national or provincial forum. It was due to that pressure and the logical arguments that two years ago floor
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

price regulations were instituted by parliament. I hope it will never be necessary to apply them. However, we know that international markets are very uncertain things, and that one cannot know what the conditions may be from day to day, or from year to year. But we do know that under that legislation our farmers, who comprise one of the finest sections in our population, under any conditions will receive satisfactory remuneration for their labour.
I have not time to discuss this matter at greater length. But I must say that our Progressive Conservative friends, and the press which supports them, would not be absolutely satisfied if price controls were entirely destroyed. They realize that those controls are necessary. Those of us who are somewhat older remember what the farmers got between 1917 and 1921. I have known a farmer along the Montreal road, for instance, who bought a farm in 1918 for $17,000, which was a reasonable price at the time, and who, after making a payment of $5,000, had to let it go because of the deflation which followed inflation. It was impossible for him to meet his payments.
We do not want a repetition of that; we want farm values to be maintained. I repeat that, generally speaking, to be succesful the farmer must possess the qualifications and abilities of a businessman, a professional man, and a financier. He knows that, of necessity, he must fight for his rights but, at the same time, he will never want anything that is not logical and practical. But I wish to make it very plain also, that he- will never want to go back to years in the past when he was the one who was paying the shot, and suffering for it.
I hold in my hand some editorials from Saturday Night. After a thorough study of the situation those who write in this periodical have come to the conclusion that, of necessity, a certain amount of control must be maintained. They go so far as to say that if, owing to the fact that the war is now over, the wartime prices and trade board should be dissolved, there would be a wish that the Minister of Finance might include in his own department a branch almost equivalent to the present wartime prices and trade board, in the matter of controls.
I shall quote only one paragraph from the Winnipeg Free Press, headed "Fighting Backwards," and stating:
The wartime prices and trade board is effecting what might be called a fighting retreat, holding each line up to the point where the rising flood of supplies makes further control unnecessary. In attempting this difficult manoeuvre it is obvious that mistakes will be made and that injustices will arise. This is inevitable.

But the over-all gain to Canada of maintaining the controls is far greater than any of the vexatious mishaps which take place from time to time. The pressure to remove the controls is very great. It comes, to far too great an extent from politicians w'ho seek an easy platform success by wanton utterance. They appeal to the narrow interests of the group they happen to be addressing and thereby neglect the national interest.
In wartime, greatly to the nation's credit, such appeals wrere ignored. They are far more dangerous to-day when the inspiration and discipline of war have vanished or grown stale. A further effort is needed.
I am going back to my constituents, and I will continue to fight for practical price control. It is not a sympathetic move; it is not popular. But I believe that in doing that I shall do my duty to my country and as a representative of my people, in speaking my mind on a question which, in my viewpoint, will be a great factor in recuperation during the post-war period.

Mr. Speaker, since May 6 we have listened to a great many speeches on this general subject. I gather from all the speeches that everyone who has spoken has his heart in the right place; he wants the same thing. The great problem arises when he tries to determine how to get it. It seems to me that we ought to face realities in a realistic fashion. We live in an age of science. Let us therefore be [DOT] scientific in our approach to the problem which is now before the house.
The matter that we are discussing has been raised by two amendments and there have been two main questions under discussion: First food production and the dangers of discouraging food production through unsuitable prices and the need for encouraging food production by suitable prices; and second the distribution of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policy and specifically the fairness or unfairness of the share of that burden being borne by the food producers of Canada or by the workers of Canada.
The amendments assume that the share of the burden at present carried by these two groups is unfair. The amendment blames the unfairness upon the government's price ceiling policies with respect to farm products and the amendment to the amendment blames the unfairness upon what it terms "the government's policies of permitting recent unjustifiable increases in the price of farm machinery and of steel". Theoretically we are now dis-

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
cussing the amendment of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum), but actually we are discussing both the amendment moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken).
In this discussion I felt that the members had a right to expect certain things. These things in large measure they did not get.
I have been disappointed. I had expected some sort of scientific approach to be used. Only about three members of those who spoke used the genuine scientific approach to the problem before us. There came into my mind certain questions. First, what is the cost of the government's price stabilization policy?
I do not recall that any member stated what the cost was. Second, who are the various classes of people in Canada who to-day are bearing a share of this burden? The producers and the workers are mentioned; call them groups "A" and "B" and tell us then what would be the other groups, "C", "D", "E", et cetera. Third, what is the share of that burden at present borne by each group, and how is that share computed? Fourth, what ought to be the share of each group, and how is the amount of that share to be computed? Fifth, to what extent does the share now borne by each group differ from the share that ought to be borne by that group, and why? Sixth, to what extent has the price increase in farm machinery and steel contributed to the difference between what each group now bears and what it ought to bear, and how? Until these questions are answered I fail to see how those who moved the amendment and the amendment to the amendment can establish their case at all.
When we turn to the Progressive Conservative amendment the house needed, in my judgment, to have the leader of the opposition name all the classes of food producers, primary and secondary, and indicate the validity of the amendment by reference to each. Probably he had in mind no such comprehensive programme, but it seemed to me that that should have come out, judging by the wording of the amendment. We ought to have been told of the situation of the producers of each of the grains, wheat, oats, barley, iye; each of the meats, beef, grass-fed and feed-lot fed; pork, mutton, poultry; each of the Canadian-grown commercial fruits, apples, pears, peaches, plums, prunes, apricots, strawberries, raspberries, grapes, loganberries; and each of the major processing vegetables, peas, beans, corn, tomatoes, as well as potatoes, milk, eggs, honey, maple products and beets for sugar-making. Until all these are dealt
with I fail to see how the leader of the opposition can establish his case, judging by the wording of the amendment.
We also ought to know what should be the price for the fishermen engaged in freshwater and salt-water fishing. Instead of having a scientific treatment of the whole case, what the members have had, as far as I can judge-and I have listened closely-is a rambling, ill-connected parliamentary talkfest, establishing hardly any fact except that something is seriously wrong with wages and prices in Canada, and tending to scarcely any conclusion other than that something drastic ought to be done about it. I believe we were all agreed on those two propositions before either the amendment or the amendment to the amendment was moved.
Just now in our national life the need is great and urgent that the members of parliament establish many important facts; that they reach many sound conclusions, and that they frame and adopt many vital policies. What we need above all things, in my judgment, in order to do these things is knowledge, detailed knowledge, and that knowledge, Mr. Speaker, at the present time is completely beyond the ordinary member of parliament. He simply cannot get it. I am not so sure but that it is beyond the cabinet ministers.
That something is very seriously wrong, we can judge by the fact that beef prices are not producing the results that we would have them produce; and by the fact of a threatened milk strike in Ontario, with literally thousands of milk producers threatening to pour their milk out on the ground or to waste it some other way unless they are given a $3 advance. These men know what it costs to produce milk, and they declare that they simply cannot produce milk at the price it is going to be, with costs as they are at the present time.
To show how serious the matter is, I am going to put on Hansard a letter in which I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) will be deeply interested. May I, in passing, congratulate the Minister of Finance because, while there is hardly a man that is more badgered than he at the present time, he is, all things considered, standing right up and taking it on the chin like a man. But just the same there are reasons for differing with some of his policies, and I am sure he realized that. This letter will be interesting to him and to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). It comes from the Lethbridge Central Feeders' Association, Lethbridge, Alberta. These people feed thousands of beef in pens every year and are consequently, I suppose, about as well equipped to pronounce

I thought that the committee would like to have that on Hansard so that they could study it. I believe that the leader of the opposition will be pleased to get that information, because it exactly supports one of the statements he made. Still, nothing is said about what to do about it, but there is the situation with respect to beef feeding in my constituency, which, I believe, is one of the finest beef-feeding areas in the country.
To see how difficult is the situation with respect to labourers, all we need to do is recall the strikes which are on at the present time or being threatened right now. According to my information, we have ,a lumber strike in British Columbia with reportedly
37,000	out; we have the seamen's union strike called for June 3, with 35,000 seamen, and a declaration that they will call out the seamen of the deep sea unless they are able to get results. There is a copper strike, according to my information, with work stopped at Anaconda America Brass Limited, New Toronto; and a rubber strike is threatened. It may be said that these conditions are to be expected at the close of a war. Those of us who have gone into matters of this kind have been impressed, I believe, with the case of these men. I personally have been greatly impressed; I have wondered how men could face life with anything like confidence while deriving such a low income from the work they were doing, and I believe something simply must be done.
I am not endeavouring to blame anybody. I am not unduly criticizing the government; I sympathize with the difficulties they are in; but then, there is the difficulty, and it is a challenge to the house. Something simply must be dona. My regret is that in all this

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
debate we have just been complaining; we have been offering no solution. In our time we are moving among conditions new and strange to see. The world is seething; we are haunted by countless anxieties; we are threatened with dreadful dangers at home and abroad. Never was there a greater need for accurate knowledge,' intensive, extensive and comprehensive, never such insistent need for courageous, realistic, epoch-making thought and action, and I submit that just such is demanded of the members of this house.
Someone will say, "Well, what has social credit to say about the question at issue? What has it to say about controls and all the rest of the questions which are being raised?" Perhaps I should give a little attention to that matter.
The social credit reaction to the questions under discussion is about as follows. First, with respect to controls, social credit does not advocate the removal of the controls too rapidly. It does not advocate maintaining controls too long. But the word which social credit likes to use in respect to controlling prices is "regulation". Regulation does not connote so much regimentation, so much threat of legal proceedings. Social credit proposes to induce fair wages and prices. There are two different ways of going about a thing: one is to force people to do it; another is to lead them to do it. Social credit believes that it is possible to organize even our society in these terrible times on the basis of inducement, and we propose to induce fair wages and prices by two main means:	first, a guarantee of equity and
stability; second, subsidies on primary production and compensating discounts on secondary products as they go into consumption, and wage bonuses. That, in brief, v is the system and 'general attitude of social credit on the matters under discussion.
With respect to prices we maintain that the price subsidy is the correct system to use. We heard with regret the government's decision to remove the two-cent subsidy on milk. We considered it a most unwise move. The government should have maintained that subsidy and enlarged and applied it far over the wide field of prices. As the days and years go by, if we are fortunate enough to see them go by without too much disaster, it will be found that the subsidy is the secret of maintaining primary production prices for every kind of primary product.
With respect to secondary products, Social Credit believes in having the government pay a portion of the retail price on such acom-modity as, for example, a binder. Consequently anyone who noticed what Social Crediters said will find that when the 12% per cent advance on machinery prices was announced, we stated, "We are not arguing that the advance should not have been made, but we are arguing that the farmers should not have had to pay it." If there had to be a 12% .per cent increase, if that had been found to be necessary, then that 12% percent increase should have been paid by direct government subsidy.
The question arises: Where will you get the money? I will discuss that point later. In the meantime, let me say this with respect to wages. Our men everywhere are dissatisfied with their wages, some justifiably so, some perhaps unjustifiably. I do not know. But where a wage increase is to be granted, that increase should take the form of a government cost of living bonus. There are some industries which are probably able to pay an increase in wages without raising prices, but all industries which are not able to do so should be assisted by the government with a definite wage bonus.
This will sound strange; it will sound epochmaking; it will sound entirely new. But just a moment's reflection on the part of hon. members must convince them that there is soundness in the proposal, because at the present time, every time labourers strike they force prices up, and when prices go up the labourers strike again to bring wages into line with prices. So that you have a vicious circle, a spiral leading to inflation, never ending.
There is only one way of dealing with that situation, namely, to determine what labourers ought to receive in any given industry, by mutual consent, study and understanding, and to see that they get it; and if the industry involved cannot pay the difference the government should. That is the social credit idea on wages.
What is the fundamental scientific approach of the social credit philosophy? First of all, social credit says: What you are to do in a nation depends entirely on your ability to produce. If you can produce enough goods of a sufficient number of kinds, you can give people pretty nearly any income which those goods can support. If you cannot produce goods, you certainly cannot have an income. If, however, you can produce goods, you ought to be able to have an income, and therefore social credit's whole approach is based on the answer to the question, how much goods can your country produce, and of how many different kinds?
Therefore the first thing that social credit would ask with respect to Canada is this. Let us have a national account book set up in
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

Canada in which we will record, with such accuracy as we can achieve, first of all actual production in'the country to-day-production of every kind what we are producing in every industry; second, what would be the capacity production? That is to say, are we producing as much as we could? If not, let that be set down. Then, what would be a reasonable estimate of potential productive capacity, considering the coal deposits, the forest wealth and all the other deposits and resources we have. What we ought to be able to produce -in the way of coal, lumber and so forth, the probable potential productive capacity, should be set down.
With that information the government would be able to draft a policy for the future, looking to increasing production and thereby raising the standard of living in the country. Having set this down as the fundamental basis upon which to work, social credit would say: You will next proceed to stimulate production to the desirable maximum, production of every kind of goods, and you should aim in a general way to make your economy as nearly self-supporting as you can. It is foolish to import rubber when you can make it; it is absurd to import sugar when you can produce it; and so on. The more nearly you can come in your economy to producing the necessities of life, the more capable you are of being independent of external influences, and the more capable you are, therefore, of governing the price structure and every other factor pertaining to the standard of living in your country. That is the general idea of social credit.
We favour a sort of national economic independence in the nation. We favour the use of our total resources, both man-power and natural or material resources, in so far as that total use is necessary to obtain the desired standard of living. If the people want a high standard they must be prepared to work in order to get it. If they do not want to work to produce, then naturally there is no income for them. Once people all over the country realize that the standard of living which they can have depends upon the amount of goods they can produce, their whole outlook on the surrounding economic situation will change.
Having stimulated production to the necessary degree, social credit says that you must stimulate consumption. There is no use in producing if you cannot consume. In normal times social credit would stimulate consumption by using wage bonuses, subsidies on prices, and by direct distributions of consumer purchasing power, taking the form of wage increases or dividends, or whatever form it may be found necessary or agreeable or desir-

able to issue it. Having taken care of the stimulation of production and consumption to the optimum degree, then social credit would say that you could raise the standard of living in Canada to the highest point consistent with Canadian production and Canadian productive capacity.	.
When social credit makes that statement it is completely in agreement with practically every speaker who has spoken in the C.C.F. organization and most of those who have spoken on both sides among the other parties. The question is, how to attain the objective? Social credit maintains that it has one or two ideas which are quite different from those advocated by any other groups in the house. Having raised the standard of living to the desirable level, social credit would say, we will now pay off the national debt with our surplus production. This is a note of hope. As far as I can make out, the concept of the Liberals and the concept of the Progressive Conservatives-I am not prepared to pronounce on the C.C.F. because they have not said very much about it-the concept of the two old line parties is this:	If you cannot
wring money out of the pockets of the taxpayers you cannot pay off the national debt, you cannot pay the interest on it.
Social credit says that is just pure nonsense, for you can pay your debt off with your goods. If you can produce enough goods you can pay your debt, provided that you manage it rightly. Then the question rises:	Can Canada produce these goods? Well, I do not think there is anyone in this house who doubts that Canada can produce enough goods in ten, fifteen or twenty years, with all her productive pow'er, to pay off her debt, and still maintain a high standard of living. But the question will be raised:	Where is the money to
come from? I wish to word very carefully what I am about to say so that every member can get its exact meaning. The money must come out of production. The commodities we can produce in excess of what the consuming public can purchase with the money they can obtain under the present debt-creating financial system-such commodities can be represented by the government with commodity dollars. The question will arise in the minds of some-I can almost see it written on the faces of some-how can you have commodity dollars? In this war we have seen developed a splendid example of commodity money. During the war the British, needing goods from members of the sterling bloc, created pounds and bought the goods they needed from the members of the sterling bloc. These members now hold these pounds. These pounds are redeemable in British goods, and just as

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
soon as the British can produce the goods to cover these pounds they will pay the members of the sterling bloc in goods and recover the pounds.	.
These pounds are not backed by gold; they are backed by British goods, both those that are produced and those that will be produced. These are commodity pounds. Commodity dollars can be created in Canada too. Such dollars created to the extent to which we have production can be used in stimulating production, financing consumption and raising the standard of living of all Canadians.
There are certain things that I think ought to be done now. I do not suppose it will do very much good to talk to the house about ideals and things to be done in the future. Let us see what we can do to-day. What can we do within the remaining weeks of this parliamentary session? These are the suggestions that I would offer. We need facts above all other things in this house to-day. Therefore we should appoint a fact-finding commission a royal commission if needs be, or fact-finding commissions, to ascertain for us in a thoroughly dependable way the information we need; and this they should do with all possible speed. I would say we should set to work a commission or as many commissions as we need to find with all possible expedition the whole truth bearing upon about eight main problems in the country: First, the production of goods in Canada; much of the argument and discussion that has gone on in this debate has been the result of insufficient knowledge, inaccurate knowledge regarding production costs. We are not in a position to get that knowledge; it is not available. A commission with such skill and of sufficient size and with sufficient money should be appointed to get that information in respect of every item of food production in this country; then everything of truth with respect to the morale and efficiency of workers. How much does a workingman need? How much ought he to have, first of all, if he is married, and, second, if he is not? How much of it should be left free of taxation? We wrangle about it in this house and nobody ever decides; nobody has any means whereby to decide. Certainly we ought to have a commission to find all these facts. Here we have the seamens union threatening a strike. Is their stand justified? Only a fact-finding body can determine the matter and give us the information with which to work. There are other topics about which we should have the full truth, namely, the justifiable cost of processing foods such as butter and cheese, canned goods, meat packing, sugar manufacturing and flour milling.
Look at the tremendous amount of talk we have had in the house -regarding what packers are able to make. What a fine thing it would be if we could have the result of a commission's investigation on this whole matter! Another matter is the cost of transportation of both freight and passengers by train tmck and bus. In the west we feel ourselves deeply aggrieved at the freight rates. We ought to know exactly to what extent we are justified in feeling aggrieved. Only a factfinding commission can determine this matter for us. We should have the facts concerning distribution, the cost of wholesaling, jobbing and retailing. We should have the cost of shelter, the cost of all kinds of building materials and of fueling. We should have the details concerning the cost of clothing. What should be the price of wool, of rayon and other clothing material? What should be the cost of processing this into the clothes that people need?
Then we should have the Canadian potential standard of living. Only a royal commission can ascertain that. We should have a national account book set up by a royal commission, showing our total potential productive capacity, and our total production, consumable or potentially consumable by Canadians, and the reductions which are essential for public service at home and abroad. Then we should have the deductions essential for servicing our debt, the deductions essential for maintaining our defence, the deductions essential for replacing capital goods and any other essentials which can be found. We should have a commission at work on this problem.
Then a commission should ascertain how we can in Canada develop the maximum consumption. Social credit has a set of proposals which, in the judgment of the Social Crediters will distribute the goods of Canada among Canadians. There are those who challenge the social credit stand; but my stand is this: If a better system than social credit cannot be found, then social credit should certainly be adopted; it certainly should be examined. It should be examined in an atmosphere in which, when a Social Crediter stands up, some silly, thoughtless creature will not shout out "25 a month", or some other idiotic expression. That is the kind of thing we hear. It is utterly impossible to have the matter fairly considered in this house.
You have never had a royal commission in Canada or anywhere else; certainly you have never had one in Canada, scientifically study social credit with the Social Crediters there to present their case. I do not think

we have ever had a careful investigation into the method of distributing the goods in the country, and yet this is the main problem which needs to be solved. We have solved the problem of production; we do not know how to distribute. The need of such a commission as I have indicated was clearly shown this afternoon by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) when I asked if he would give us a list of the goods which are in short supply. The minister foresaw that he would not be able to answer that question because he did not know where he could turn to get that information. In my judgment that is the very thing the minister ought to be able to turn to without hesitating a second. We ought to know the goods which are in short supply in this country. We ought to know why they are in short supply. We do not know that. How in the world can we go about scientific housekeeping in this country when we know so little about the essentials?
I maintain that Canada should forthwith begin to prepare to put her house in order. It is high time that Canadians as a wThole found out just where they stand.

He advocated that policy in peace time, and it has something to commend it.
One of the suggestions I want to reply to is that this policy which is now in effect is a prices board policy. Strong citicism was made by one speaker yesterday or the day before- I read it in Hansard this morning-that the present policy is the prices board policy and that because it is a prices board policy put into effect by Mr. Gordon it ought to be opposed by this house, partly for that reason and partly because those making the statement believed that it was not a sound policy.
I wish to point out that the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) in relation to the prices board and particularly myself and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) have no foundation whatsoever in fact. The fact is that in the first three years of this war I advocated continuously that that policy which had been followed prior to the war and which served the purpose prior to the war was serving no purpose whatsoever during the war except to keep down the price of cattle to farmers who had cattle to sell in the fall. Why? In the period preceding the war we could not get a market for our cattle readily in the fall of the year. Therefore we asked people to take those cattle and feed them over until the spring. The price was depressed, not by design and not by the fact that there was any particular policy in that regard but simply because there were so many cattle on the market. Those who fed those cattle in the winter months did not make as much money in the spring as people are now trying to tell us they would make if we did the same thing over again.
When the war came what happened? After 1942, particularly, we had a market for everyone of our cattle that could be put on the market in any part of Canada. All one had to do to sell cattle was to offer them for sale and they were all sold

We were told a few moments ago by the hon. member for Lethbridge that feeders, in order to buy cattle last October and November, had to go into the markets and bid against the packers; in other words, bid against the butchers whether they were packers or not. Why? Because there was a market for every pound of beef that came on the market ready to kill.
There is no one in this house who knows anything about farmers' returns who would suggest that every farmer who put on the market last fall a good butcher steer ought to take a cent or a cent and a half or two cents a pound less for it than the ceiling price made possible, in order that some farmer or some feed-lot operator near some city could take those cattle, buy grain and feed them over the *winter and put them on the market next spring a little heavier in weight.

Therefore the farmer who was bringing his cattle on the market in the fall had to take a price under the low ceiling in order that someone else could get the cattle one and a half to two cents lower than the spring price. That is the policy advocated by the feed-lot supporters now. I had a group of representatives of these feed-lot men in my office the other day, and two out of the five expressed themselves most strongly, before leaving the office, as opposed to the policy proposed and saying that the present policy was superior after it had been explained to them.
The situation does not need to be proven by anything I say with regard to it. All one has to do is to take the figures. Members on both sides of the house have been saying that what we want is stabilized prices. To go back to 1928, the average price was $10.40. The price went down to $9.10 and up to $11.48. If one takes one of the years in the middle of the depression the average price then was $5.93. The price went down to $5.60 and went up as high as $6.23.
If one takes different years preceding the war and during the early part of the war, one finds that the average from 1926 to 1929 was $9.04 for good steers at Toronto; for 1928-to go back to the year we were discussing a few moments ago-it was $11.48; for 1920 it was $12.89, the variations running

all the way from $12.89 down to $9.04 back in that period in which, we sometimes say, farmers enjoyed the greatest prosperity prior to the present time.
To come to 1941, about a year and a half after the war started, the price went down from the average of $9.04 back in those years and of $10.48 back in 1928, to $8.70. At an earlier time, just prior to the war, it had been higher than that. In 1942 it went up to $10.29. It was in 1941 and 1942 that we were having these discussions as between the prices board and the Department of Agriculture. After two years of discussions, after all these men who run the feed-lots and all those who run feeding farms in eastern Canada and those who run these small farms across Canada had had delegations in and discussed the matter, we finally, two and a half years ago. convinced everyone that the present policy was more likely to bring about stabilization and give good returns to the farmers than the policy which had been followed throughout the years preceding the war and during the early part of the war. We argued it on the ground that there is a market every day of the year with war and since we began selling beef to Britain for every pound of beef that is put on the market.
Why should there be a variation in price under those circumstances? If farmers have beef to market every day of the' 365 days and people want to eat all the meat every day, why should there be any variation in price or holding for better prices? The only reason there was that the variation before was because the supply was greater than the demand. Let me say to my hon. friends on the other side who are inclined to scoff at the idea of supply and demand, that the law of supply and demand has operated ever since there have been men on the face of this earth who have made any records; supply and demand will continue to operate, and anyone who loses sight of that fact is going to get into trouble sooner or later. When supply and demand were more or less balanced, as they were during the war period, what was the position? The average price in 1943 was $11.46; in 1944. $11.48; in 1945, $11.65. There has been a variation from $11.46 to $11.65 during those three years of stabilization, and prices are higher than the average price obtained in any other continuous three years since 1914. We went through the last period advocating stabilization of prices and came through with the most successful system of stabilization of farm prices that this country or any other country has ever had and because of that we were sent back here to carry on the policy.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) the other day, the hon. gentleman said that India had a poor crop; that the people are starving there; that the people are starving in North Africa and South Africa; that the people are starving in France and starving in some other countries. Well there are two or three reasons why they are starving in most of those countries; but there is one reason in every one of them and that is that they had a crop failure last year. In India they had one of the most complete crop failures they

have ever experienced, with low production; in North and South Africa they had one of the greatest crop failures they have ever experienced, with low production; and one could enumerate other areas in which there is the greatest difficulty in relation to food at the present time.
Why is it that when persons are calling attention to these facts they refuse, when they come to Canada, to say that we have had three of the poorest crops in certain wheatgrowing areas, the last three, that we have ever experienced? Hon. gentlemen who come from the southwestern part of Saskatchewan know that this year the people are receiving payments under prairie farm assistance in greater amounts than in any other year but one in the whole history of the act since 1939 up to the present time. Why? Because they have a poor crop; and when we admit that every other country is in difficulties which has had a poor crop, why can we not be honest with ourselves and say that Canada is in difficulties in delivering greater quantities of food too because she had a poor crop in the grain-growing area during the last year; not quite so poor the year before, but still poor, and poorer the year before that?
Why cannot we be more honest with ourselves and say that in the week before the week that has just gone by authorities reported that we had in Canada the poorest prospects that we have ever had in the same week in twenty-four years. Why cannot we be honest with ourselves and say these things? And let us say them to the world, and not tell people that no matter what the weather is like we are going to have a good crop this year; that all we have to do is to put in more acreage, and do more of this and the government do something and we shall have a crop just because they say so. I have said that a week ago we had the poorest condition for twenty-four years, but I do not want the house to come to the conclusion that we are bound to have the poorest crop we have had in twenty-four years. Every western member knows that if we have three good rains in June and have them properly distributed we shall grow a crop in spite of everything that has happened up to the present. With the conditions we have to-day, if we do not have those three rains, if we do not have at least two of them, we shall be talking next fall about difficulties similar to those that we have experienced before. We in this country have to take our own history into consideration.
When our hon. friends were considering this matter within the last week this suggestion was made: you ought to increase your wheat acreage seven per cent for the whole
world in order to produce so many bushels of wheat during the next year. During the last three years we have increased our wheat acreage in Canada by over fifty per cent, and we have not had as much wheat in any one of the years during which we had the increased acreage as we had in the year preceding that. Therefore I think we should face the facts and simply admit that in this country we depend upon good weather to produce feed grain. This is a country where we must feed live stock for seven months of the year. We depend upon feed grain to finish our live stock and get food upon our own markets and also to be able to export food to other countries. If we get it we shall be able to help; if we do not get it we shall be in the position in which some other countries find themselves this year. Take South Africa. South Africa is the most like this country of any country that is producing wheat to place upon the markets of the world. I sat in Washington yesterday and listened to the representative of South Africa review a story that was so nearly like our story of the thirties that one would almost believe he was talking about this country. He said: "Two years ago we thought we were goiilg to be able to help solve the problem of food shortage throughout the world. But to-day we find that instead of helping with it we are asking for food from other parts of the world."
Their area is like ours; it is a dry area. The only areas in which you can produce No. 1 hard wheat are dry ones. I do not think that can be repeated too often. No. 1 hard wheat is a good food to be utilized for dealing with situations such as we have now, because it will keep for ten or twenty years in a good bin. If you grow too much of it this year you can pass it around some years hence. We are trying to find some kind of policy that will not only stabilize prices, but do something else which is essential to the stabilization of prices, namely, stabilize distribution, so that you can carry over your big crops into a period when there is going to be a shortage instead of throwing them on the market and pressing the prices down. If we can do that we can not only stabilize prices to our farmers but also stabilize the distribution in order that fewer people will suffer from hunger throughout the world. If we recognize these facts we shall get along much quicker with the solution of our problems.

To that motion an amendment was moved by myself and an amendment to the amendment by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) representing the C.C.F. party.
On a motion to go into supply opportunity is given to members to raise matters of major public concern or to bring forward any grievances from the electorate in any part of Canada or to discuss any other matter of public interest. The amendment I proposed raises two major matters of public interest. May I say in passing that many members have spoken of it as a non-confidence motion. Mr. Speaker any amendment moved to a government motion the speech from the throne or the budget or supply is of course a lack of confidence motion. In that connection I may say that this motion was not moved with any expectation of dislodging the government or in any attempt to do so. It was moved with the intention of bringing before the house and the government and the country two major questions of public policy, which I think are very important and, with all respect, very clear in the amendment that I moved.
Before I read the amendment may I say one or two things with respect to the debate so far. It has covered a very wide range,
and I agree with some of those who have said that much of the debate had no direct bearing either on the amendment or on the amendment to the amendment. I propose in my remarks to-night to deal wholly with the amendment, and with the amendment to the amendment, but chiefly with the former. Before I do so may I refer briefly to two or three of the addresses we have heard to-night?
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), in his remarks, answered partly a question I asked him the other day when he was on his estimates or on going into supply. I asked him to give a statement of the prices paid to farmers for the major agricultural products in Canada, and with it a statement of prices paid to farmers in the United States-prices paid under comparable conditions here and across the line in the United States. To-night he quoted prices on butter and cheese and indicated that they were approximately the same in the two countries.

After much debate in this house, so far as wheat is concerned, one does not need to quote again the difference in price as between the United States and Canada. It is a very great difference. In his remarks the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) dealt with two questions, first, the necessity of production if we are to increase our standard of living in this country, and, second, the value of subsidies as an equalizing force in our economy. He said that he favoured subsidies as a means of equalizing the returns to different sections of our economy. With practically all that he had to say regarding production I am in agreement. I could not follow him clearly with respect to his support of subsidies, but even there I could go with him part way.
