I am simply giving the explanation; hon. members may take it or not. I repeat:

with respect to farm products are discouraging production of needed food . . .
That is one of the two sections of the amendment. What was the other? This is it: -and imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
That is all there is in the amendment-these two statements. They are either correct or incorrect. If they are incorrect I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) will present the government's side, showing, as well as he can, that they are incorrect. If they are correct it is a serious indictment of the policies themselves or of the administration of the policies. I am inclined to criticize the administration of the policies more than the policies themselves, because you cannot raise the price of one commodity which enters into the cost of others without creating inequities. That is the position we are taking.
With respect to the observation that speakers have talked about other things, let me say, Mr. Speaker, that there is nothing in this amendment about taking the lid off controls; there is nothing about allowing prices to go sky-high; there is nothing about uncontrolled inflation; there is no attack on the principle of trying to control inflation. There is nothing in the amendment save this, that the combination of the government's price control policies and its administration of them during recent months is discouraging production of needed food in a time of famine ; and to the extent that these policies and the administration of them increase farm costs more than they do farm prices they discourage the production of food in a time like this.
Mr. Speaker, these are major questions. We take the position that we want production. We take the position that we want equity between producers and workers and business and industry. If this amendment refers only to the producers of food on the farms of Canada it is not because of any favour desired for farmers but rather that they shall not be denied equity in our economy. We hold that recent policies put them in a relatively inequitable position. I shall deal with the merits of the matter in a moment.
The first question is: Is the production of agricultural products going down in Canada or not? It will not be enough to show that production is going down to prove that it is because of the government's price policies. Weather conditions affect the yield of crops; but surely there is no one in this house who

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
will say that price does not affect production also. Price gave us production of industrial equipment in the war. The advance of almost unlimited credit to industry, together with cost-plus contracts, and priorities in needed supplies gave producers the incentive to produce and they did produce. However we may criticize details, they got production on a scale that we are all proud of. But we are not applying as generous policies now toward getting production of food in a time of famine. As a matter of fact, the government's policies are working the other way, because some of these price ceilings on non-farm products- some of the farm costs-have been raised more rapidly than the prices of farm products.
Let me deal with the question of production of food on farms. The major farm products of Canada may be grouped in two; grain or cereals, and live stock products of various kinds. There are many other lines, of course, but I cannot now deal with all. I need not discuss the production of cereals. We discussed all that a while ago. The government's policy was then clearly stated. They did not favour any increase in the acreage of wheat. It is true that the acreage of wheat has gone up, but not as a result of government policy; it has gone up in spite of government policy, gone up by taking some of the acreage that would go into coarse grains, part of which would go to feed live stock, gone up because some of the summer-fallow acreage has been put into wheat.
Let me now deal with the production of live stock products and see what is happening in Canada. Our position is that production is going down, and that the government's price policies tend to discourage production. Some speakers said that over the last ten years the production of food in Canada increased. It did. This country is gettting more populous every year, and in the last five of those ten years we had good weather most of the time. During that period, and particularly during the last three or four years, we had the incentive of favourable prices, and in the war years we had the added incentive of patriotism. Farmers were working harder, working longer hours; older men returned to help; farmers' wives and children all helped, and I include also the incentive of a favourable relative position of prices of farm products to cost, during the last three years. Taken together, that combination gave us a large production.
But what is happening now? The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) said he was quoting reports of the bureau of statistics. Any figures I quote here are taken from official documents of the government.
There can be no purpose in trying to misinterpret statistics. Anyone who attempts that sort of thing will soon be caught up with. Let us have only what the truth is. What do they say? In connection with creamery butter our production in 1944 was 298,000,000 pounds and in 1945 it was 293,000,000 pounds, a reduction of only two per cent. In 1944 we slaughtered 8-8 million hogs; in 1945 we slaughtered 5-7 million, a reduction of 33 per cent.
And what is happening in more recent months? That is what we are concerned with. Now that the war is over and we are getting back to peace-time conditions, changes are being made every litttle while by the government or its officials. What is happening now? From January to March of this year, as compared with January to March of last year, our production of butter shows a reduction of 18 per cent; our production of factory cheese shows a reduction of 33 per cent; our production of concentrated milk products shows a reduction of 9 per cent; the number of hogs slaughtered show's a reduction of 50 per cent as compared with 1944 and of 33 per cent as compared with 1945. That is not a completely accurate interpretation of what w'ill happen during the whole year but it is a pretty good guide. For the rest of the year pastures will help out production, and differences will not be as great; but those are the latest figures we have, and that is what they show-a steadily declining production.
' I have taken the trouble to add up the production, the total weight, of creamery butter, factory cheese, concentrated milk products, dressed weight of inspected slaughter of live stock products, including hogs, cattle, calves, sheep and lambs. What does this show? In 1944 the total produced was, in round figures, 2,900 million pounds. In 1945 it was 2.700 million pounds. But what about January, February and March of this year as compared with the same period last year and the year before? In 1944 the total was 716 million pounds; in 1945 it was 632 million pounds, and in 1946 it was 502 million pounds, a reduction this year of 30 per cent as compared with two years ago and of 20 per cent as compared with last year.
I have admitted, Mr. Speaker, that increasing disparities in prices and cost may not cause all that reduction. Weather and coarse grain supply help; but price is a major factor, and increasing costs do discourage plans for production.
I come now to the next point, but before I deal with it let me read the amendment

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
COMMONS moved by the C.C.F. The resolution moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government's policies

of what?
-of permitting recent unjustifiable increases in the prices of farm machinery and of steel have resulted in imposing on food producers and workers . . .
The rest is the same. How does that change the original amendment? It takes out of my amendment the whole question of the effect of the recent administration of these price ceiling policies on production. It removes that entirely from the immediate question before us. And that was the major economic question I wished to have this house discuss. It is important to know whether the policies being followed by the government and administered by the government are discouraging production.
I have no objection in the world to the C.C.F. bringing forward a motion such as this and discussing it on its merits. Are these increases in the prices of farm machinery and steel unjustified? On one ground I would agree that they are. They are .^justified in so far as they increase farmers' costs without increasing farmers' prices. On other grounds I leave it to the government to bring forward evidence to show that these increases were justified. It may be they can do so. I imagine they have that evidence, or they would not have put the increases into effect. I expect they will show that the cost of producing that machinery and that steel,. whether as a result of the increased cost of labour or of raw material, or whatever it be. has so gone up that enterprise would not risk its capital to produce goods and to give employment if it were not likely to have enough returns to pay those additional costs for labour and materials. If the government can show that, then responsible members will not have much choice but to accept its decision. But I suggest that this is an amendment which might have been brought in by itself. As it is, it discards altogether the heart of my amendment, which I submit is a proper and an important economic question for discussion and decision, not necessarily on party lines though, as this house is constituted, probably that is too much to expect.
Then the C.C.F. amendment goes farther and says these things:
. . . have resulted in imposing on food producers and workers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
I have no objection to the words "and workers" being put in, but I wonder what farmers

will think of people who frame an amendment which suggests that food producers are not workers.
I have dealt with the question of whether or not production is going down. In this connection I should like to read from a report of the Ontario department of agriculture dated May 14:
Production of butter by Ontario creameries in . the first four months of 1946 was down more than 1,500 tons as compared with the output in the same period last year, the Ontario department of agriculture said to-day in its monthly dairy report.
Cumulative output of creamery butter for the first four months was 15,327,400 pounds against 18,806,400 for the same period last year. Butter production in April, 1946, was 5,352,100 pounds against 6,117,500 for April, 1945. Stocks of creamery butter in storage warehouses throughout the province up to May 1 was 1,064,400 pounds against 1,478,000 in the same period of last year.
Then it goes on to give similar figures showing decreases in the production of cheese, but 1 shall not take time to put more of the statement on the record.	.
I have been dealing with the question: Is production going down?
I wish now to deal as briefly as I can with the question of recent price ceiling decisions in their relation to equity for farmers. The. point is:	Are price ceilings, as now being administered by the government, affecting unfairly the producers of this country? Are they or are they not? If not, then that section of my amendment should not be supported. If they are, then it should be supported.
What are the facts? I have here a statement showing the dates when all these price ceilings were established, a statement of the date of the last subsidies, and what they were.
At this late hour I shall not take time to deal with all of them, but if I were to make a brief summary of them, it would be this:	Except
for minor changes, the majority of price ceilings and subsidies in farm products have been constant for two or three years. There have been some minor increases in recent months, of course-indeed, there have been two or three small increases since this debate started. Sometimes I have wondered why there was this long delay in proceeding with the motion which was moved some two and one-half weeks ago.
I have said that except for minor changes, the majority of price ceilings and subsidies on farm produce-have been constant for two or three years. The policy of this government with respect to price ceilings in the early years of the war was to fasten upon agriculture a level of prices 20 per cent below parity, and it remained that way for some years, even under serious protests from

House of Commons
organized agriculture, and from every student of agriculture. About three years ago that condition was changed. I shall not go into the question of why. Perhaps rising world prices helped. An hon. member of the C.C.F. has said it was because of victories by their candidates in the west. But I have sometimes had the notion it was because in December of 1942 the official opposition took a stand for a square deal for all agriculture, as a start to raise the price of wheat from 90 cents to S1.25-which was done by the government the very next year.
I may say to the house that at no time except the last three years has agriculture had anything like a square deal at any time since the last war-only in those three years. On the basis of what some called parity-and it is parity only in one narrow technical sense, but not real parity-it was well treated in those three years. But on the basis of real parity, that is a farmer receiving a fair proportion of the nation's income, it has not had that kind of parity even in those three years.
